equation.locator: NASEM 2023 DRI for Energy (PMID 36693139; NCBI Bookshelf NBK588659): Summary, Table S-1 p.4 (adult TEE equations; units footnote), Table S-2 pp.6-7 (EER for ages 0-18.99 y with energy cost of growth), Tables S-5 and S-6 (lactation), p.11 (two-step planning); Ch. 5 p.68 and Table 5-1 p.72 (8,600-observation database), p.70 (PAL > 2.5 excluded), p.71 (IOM-database adults with normal weight, overweight or obesity; BMI < 18.5 excluded), p.76 (BMI-subset models), Table 5-4 p.82 (PAL bands, including 14-18.99 y), p.86 and Table 5-6 (adult n and fit; underweight/extreme-obesity sensitivity; FFM/FM model), p.87 (BMI slope test); Ch. 7 pp.146-147 (two-step method; no valid PAL classification tool)
equation.note:
This is the current US/Canada DRI and replaces the IOM 2005 EER. The equations predict total energy expenditure (TEE, which equals EER in weight-stable adults) from sex, age, height, weight and a physical-activity category. The combined doubly-labelled-water (DLW) database held 8,600 observations across all life stages (Ch. 5 p.68; Table 5-1 p.72). The adult equations' fit is reported on 1,016 men and 1,342 women (Table 5-6, p.86). Height and weight slopes did not differ between normal-weight and overweight/obese adults (p.87). Underweight adults were in the general fit, and removing them together with BMI > 40 did not change model performance (p.86). But their accuracy was not reported separately, the slope test did not include them, and the IOM part of the database excluded BMI < 18.5 (p.71). So the set is shown to cover normal weight, overweight and obesity; treat underweight as less certain. Do not mix these equations with IOM 2005 or FAO 2004 PAL bands: the same label means a different multiplier in each system (see contradictions).

Users the adult equations do not cover (cross-group flags for the safety group):
(a) Pregnancy. The adult equations exclude it. IOM 2009 sets a positive weekly gain for every pre-pregnancy BMI group and gives no safe rate of loss (findings 748, 749, 751). safety.exclusions must list pregnancy so that safety_block withholds targets.
(b) Lactation. The adult equations exclude it (NASEM adds milk-production and mobilisation terms, Tables S-5 and S-6), and no verified finding covers a deficit while breastfeeding (open question). safety.exclusions must list lactation until that is resolved.
(c) BMI below 18.5. Fat loss for these users should be blocked by a safety BMI floor (17.5 vs 18.5 is an open contradiction; findings 472, 39). The engine has no BMI check today.

Limits:
(1) Age. The adult equations cover ages 19+. For under-19s NASEM uses separate EER equations with an energy-cost-of-growth term (+20 kcal/d at 14-18.99 y; Summary Table S-2) and separate 14-18.99 y PAL bands (Table 5-4). These were read in the saved NAP text but are not in the verified findings. safety.minimumAgeYears is 18, so the owner must decide how an 18-year-old is handled: apply the adult equations as an owner decision, add the 14-18.99 y equations as verified findings, or raise the minimum age to 19. Pontzer 2021 (finding 126, a single pooled-DLW study) puts the start of the adult TEE plateau at about 20.5 y (95% CI 19.8-21.2), with 20-25-year-olds averaging 102.7% of the adult-expected value. The adult equation therefore probably underestimates an 18-year-old by a few percent (app inference). That makes a deficit slightly larger than intended, and the weight-trend correction (finding 50) must catch it. Also, the engine's age_years() takes the difference in calendar years, so it can count a user up to one year older than they are, and a 17-year-old can pass an 18-year minimum. The effect on the EER is small (at most 10.83 kcal/d for men, 7.01 for women), but the admission effect is a safety-group issue.
(2) PAL above 2.5 was excluded (finding 55; Ch. 5 p.70), so heavy endurance trainers will be underestimated even at veryActive. Do not cap their intake at the veryActive EER.
(3) NASEM says no valid, reliable tool exists to classify an individual's PAL category (Ch. 7 p.147). The EER is only a starting point. The report's two-step method is to compute the EER, then monitor weight and adjust intake (finding 50; Summary p.11; Ch. 7 p.146).
(4) No body-composition term. NASEM's own FFM/FM-based adult model did only slightly better than the weight-based one (Ch. 5 p.86). In muscular physique athletes, weight-based RMR equations underestimated measured RMR by 4.5-15.1% (finding 100). An athlete meta-analysis found Mifflin-St Jeor, Owen and FAO/WHO/UNU equations significantly biased and imprecise (finding 76; the verified finding gives no direction of bias). Whether this carries over to the EER is untested (low certainty).

Coefficients and the Ch. 5 text were re-checked against the saved NAP read-online text on 2026-09-24. Review: accepted the objections on adult sample size, the FFM/FM model, the direction of finding 76, 18-year-old handling, the age calculation and the pregnancy exclusion. The objection that underweight adults are outside the validation range was only partly accepted, because p.86 shows underweight observations were in the general fit. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #43, #44, #45, #47, #50, #55, #76, #100, #126, #748, #749, #751, #472, #39.

eerCoefficients.locator: NASEM 2023 DRI for Energy: Summary Table S-1 p.4 (men and women 19+ y; units footnote), repeated in Table S-3 pp.7-8; Summary p.11 (worked example); Ch. 5 p.68 (database), Table 5-6 p.86 (adult n and fit), p.87 (BMI slope test), Table 5-10 p.92 (external validation)
eerCoefficients.note: Use as TEE (kcal/d) = intercept + age*years + heightCm*cm + weightKg*kg. The age coefficient is negative (-10.83 for men, -7.01 for women), and the male veryActive intercept is negative (-517.88). All 32 coefficients match the published values (saved NAP Summary Table S-1, re-checked programmatically on 2026-09-24). The footnote gives the units: kcal/d, age in years, weight in kg, height in cm. For weight-stable adults EER = TEE (Table S-3 note). Published fit (Table S-1; Table 5-6): men n 1,016, R2 0.73, RMSE 339 kcal/d, MAPE 9.4%; women n 1,342, R2 0.71, RMSE 246 kcal/d, MAPE 8.7%. External validation (65 studies, 5,056 people) compared cohort-mean predicted TEE with observed TEE across 144 cohorts: r 0.92 for men (32 cohorts) and 0.93 for women (71 cohorts), with RMSE 222 and 169 kcal/d (Table 5-10, p.92). This is cohort-level agreement and overstates individual accuracy, so use energy.predictionErrorKcal for individual error. Test case from the report: a 22-year-old, 165-cm, 63-kg low-active woman gives 2,275 kcal/d (Summary p.11; these coefficients give 2,275.37). Pair these only with the NASEM 2023 PAL bands in energy.activityLevels. Review: objection accepted (validation r is cohort-level; locator completed). Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #43, #44.

value.title: Inactive

value.title: Low active
value.description: Everyday living plus about 60-80 min of walking at 3-4 mph (about 4.8-6.4 km/h) each day. Typical PAL about 1.6.

value.title: Active
value.description: Everyday living plus, each day, about 30-50 min of walking at 3-4 mph (about 4.8-6.4 km/h), 45 min of moderate cycling and 40 min of doubles tennis. Typical PAL about 1.75.

value.description: Everyday living plus, each day, about 45 min of moderate cycling, about 25 min of jogging at 10 min per mile (about 6.2 min/km) and 60 min of doubles tennis. Typical PAL about 2.05.

activityLevels.locator: NASEM 2023 DRI for Energy: Ch. 5, p.80 (derivation), Tables 5-3 and 5-4 p.82 (PAL cut-offs), p.70 (PAL > 2.5 exclusion); Ch. 7, p.147 (inactive definition; classification limits) and Table 7-1 p.148 with its text (category labels, activity examples, substitution, office-work caveat)
activityLevels.note: The titles are NASEM's category labels (Table 7-1). They are required, because diet_view.diet_options reads level['title'] for every level and would raise a KeyError without them. palMin is inclusive and palMax exclusive, as published (for example 1.53 <= PAL < 1.68). The cut-offs are the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of DLW PAL (observed plus predicted) in adults aged 19-70 (n 4,299), and they apply at all adult ages (finding 45; Ch. 5 p.80; Tables 5-3 and 5-4, p.82). They are high certainty and were checked against Table 5-4 and the Table 7-1 note. The engine never computes with palMin or palMax. The user picks a level from its title and description, and those come from Table 7-1, which NASEM offers only as a descriptive guide (finding 46, low certainty). The object is therefore graded low, the more conservative grade for the part the app uses. In Table 7-1 the activities within a category are added together on top of daily living: NASEM sums active as 30-50 min of moderate activity plus about 85 min of vigorous activity, and very active as more than 2 h of vigorous activity. NASEM adds that other activities can be substituted, since the examples show only amount and intensity. It also says the examples may suit mainly people in low-exertion jobs such as office work (p.148). The inactive wording follows NASEM: minimally active beyond daily living, with little or no occupational activity (p.147). The mph and min/mile values are converted to metric by arithmetic only (3-4 mph = 4.8-6.4 km/h; 10 min/mile = 6.2 min/km). NASEM says step counts and questionnaires correlate only weakly with DLW PAL, that meeting activity guidelines cannot place a person in a category, and that no valid, reliable tool classifies an individual (p.147). The app should therefore say the choice is approximate and rely on the weight-trend correction (finding 50). Table 7-1 does not map resistance-training sessions onto PAL (open question). PAL above 2.5 is outside the equations' range (finding 55; Ch. 5 p.70). Do not use the IOM 2005 (1.4/1.6/1.9) or FAO 2004 (1.70/2.00) bands with these equations. Review: accepted both objections. The title field and the low grade come from the second objection; the km/h correction, the substitution and office-work caveats and NASEM's inactive wording come from the first. The first objection's moderate grade was not kept, because the app uses only the low-certainty descriptions. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #45, #46, #55, #50.

predictionErrorKcal.locator: NASEM 2023 DRI for Energy: Ch. 5, 'Prediction Error' and Table 5-8, p.89 (SEPV, adults 19+ y); Ch. 7, pp.152-153 (interpretation and worked example); Summary p.12 (68%/95% interpretation)
predictionErrorKcal.note: Standard error of the predicted value (SEPV) in kcal/d, checked against Table 5-8 in the saved NAP text. NASEM gives it for an individual at the stratum's average age, height and weight with an active PAL: men 50.3 y, 175.9 cm, 83.1 kg (predicted TEE 2,930 kcal/d); women 53.9 y, 162.3 cm, 71.9 kg (2,281 kcal/d). It therefore varies somewhat with a user's characteristics. NASEM's reading is that about 68% of people have a true requirement within +/-1 SEPV of their EER, and almost everyone (about 95%) within +/-1.96 SEPV. That is +/-670 kcal/d for men and +/-472 for women (computed). Report example: a woman with EER 2,275 kcal/d has a 68% range of 2,034-2,516 kcal/d and a 95% range of 1,803-2,747 kcal/d (Ch. 7 p.152). The published model RMSE is similar (men 339, women 246 kcal/d; Table S-1). App inference, not stated by NASEM: the SEPV is equation error given the correct PAL category, so a wrongly chosen category adds error and the displayed band is a lower bound on uncertainty. Suggested UI: show the target as an estimate with a +/-1 SEPV band. Review: objection accepted (page locators, stated covariates, inference labelled). kcalPerGram.note: This is an official report without a DOI or PMID: ISBN 92-5-105212-3, ISSN 1813-3932 (both checked on the FAO report page). The text gives average metabolizable energy for a mixed diet, after allowing for intestinal absorption and the unoxidised nitrogen of protein: 16.7 kJ (4 kcal)/g for carbohydrate and protein and 37.7 kJ (9 kcal)/g for fat (re-read in the saved FAO text). Ethanol is 29.3 kJ (7 kcal)/g in the same section, which matches ACSM 2016 (finding 216) if alcohol logging is added. When a food record already carries an analysed energy value (for example FoodData Central), use that value rather than recomputing it from grams. No reviewer objection; unchanged from the draft. tissueKcalPerKgBodyMass.rationale:
No official report or synthesis gives one energy value per kg of body-mass change. The published values depend on body fat, sex and time on the diet, so 7,700 kcal/kg (the 3,500 kcal/lb rule, 32.2 MJ/kg; findings 524, 525) is an owner decision. The reasoning:

(1) Energy stored in tissue lost after the first month ranges from about 4,900 to over 9,300 kcal/kg. CALERIE (Heymsfield 2012; 23 overweight adults) measured a cumulative 6,041 +/- 376 (SEM) kcal/kg at week 6, with no significant change to week 24 (finding 547). Kiel's 13-week very-low-calorie diet gave 6,119 kcal/kg in men and 6,804 in women (finding 548). Hall 2008's modified-Forbes model gives about 24.7 MJ/kg (about 5,900 kcal/kg) when 15 kg is lost from 20 kg of initial fat. It finds the fixed rule roughly valid only when initial fat exceeds about 30 kg; below that the rule overestimates the deficit needed, significantly so below about 25 kg (findings 524, 525). Tissue densities are 9,300 kcal/kg for fat and 1,100 for fat-free mass (findings 550, 557, 818). Resistance-trained dieting men lost a mean 28.7% of lost weight as lean mass (range 12-54%; systematic review, finding 233), which gives about 6,950 kcal/kg (0.713 x 9,300 + 0.287 x 1,100), with a range of about 4,900-8,300. Trained women kept lean mass on average, which gives about 9,300 kcal/kg or more.

(2) The intake change needed per kg of loss is larger than the tissue energy, because expenditure falls as weight falls. TEE drops about 94-100 kJ/d (about 22-24 kcal/d) per kg lost (finding 534), adaptive thermogenesis adds about 220 kcal/d (finding 53), and the thermic effect of food (about 10% of expenditure; finding 56) falls with intake. Sanghvi 2015 studied non-obese CALERIE adults with a linearised model whose weight-derived intake changes matched DLW/DXA intake-balance values at group level. The model uses an effective rho of 8,840 +/- 450 kcal/kg (findings 552, 553). The owner reads the gap between rho and tissue energy as this fall in expenditure; Sanghvi does not break rho down this way. There is also a direct test: in seven supervised trials over about 1-3 months, deficits sized with the 3,500 kcal/lb rule produced 20.1 lb of loss against 27.6 lb predicted (finding 544).

(3) Safety direction. For fat loss, a larger factor gives a larger deficit. 7,700 is below the 8,840 intake-conversion value, and by the Thomas 2013 test deficits sized with it produce slower loss than targeted on average, so the first deficit errs small. The tissue-only values for lean users and men (about 5,900-6,950) would give smaller deficits still. But they ignore the expenditure fall in (2) and would push realised loss further below target for most users. They would add no safety beyond the engine's energy floor (safety.minimumEnergyKcal, safety.maximumDeficitFractionOfTEE, safety.energyAvailabilityFloorKcalPerKgFFM) and the goals.fatLoss.maxWeeklyLossFraction check. The transient early values (about 2,500-5,500 kcal/kg in the first 1-4 weeks, mostly glycogen, protein and water; findings 547, 551) are not used, because they would under-dose almost every user.

(4) NASEM uses the EER only as a starting point and then adjusts intake from the weight trend (finding 50), so this factor sets only the first offset. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #525, #524, #547, #548, #551, #233, #557, #818, #550, #552, #553, #544, #537, #534, #53, #56, #50, #273.

weeklyChangeFraction.locator: Ruiz-Castellano C et al. 2021, Nutrients 13(9):3255: Abstract; Section 3 Energy Intake (case studies: FFM kept better at 0.5 than at 0.7 or 1.0%/wk); Section 9 Conclusions and Practical Applications. Corroborated by Helms ER et al. 2014, JISSN 11:20 (doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20): Abstract, 'Caloric intake for competition', Table 1. Deficit limits: ACSM/AND/DC 2016, MSSE 48(3) p.548 (<1%/wk; 250-500 kcal/d); Murphy & Koehler 2022, Scand J Med Sci Sports 32(1):125, PubMed abstract.
weeklyChangeFraction.note:
Unit: signed fraction of body mass per week (-0.005 = lose 0.5%/wk). The engine turns this value into the daily energy offset (fraction x body mass x energy.tissueKcalPerKgBodyMass / 7), so in practice it is the prescribed deficit.

Changed from the draft's -0.007. Reviewers split: one objection kept -0.007 and disclosed the conflict, the other moved to -0.005. I accepted -0.005. The %-body-mass sources and the kcal-deficit sources conflict (a listed contradiction), the task rule is to take the more conservative value for a safety-related parameter, and the cited findings support it. -0.005 is the lower bound of the 0.5-1.0%/wk range in Ruiz-Castellano 2021 and Helms 2014. Both are narrative reviews, so this is graded low.

Reasons: (1) In the Ruiz-Castellano case studies, fat-free mass was kept better at 0.5%/wk than at 0.7 or 1%/wk (low quality). (2) At the static 7,700 kcal/kg rule (my arithmetic), -0.007 means about 460 kcal/d at 60 kg, 580 at 75 kg and 850 at 110 kg. That is above ACSM 2016's own 250-500 kcal/d starting deficit for most adults. It is above the ~500 kcal/d at which the Murphy & Koehler 2022 meta-regression (abstract only) found that deficits abolished lean-mass gains from resistance training. Above ~100 kg it is also above AHA 2013's 500-750 kcal/d. At -0.005 the figures are about 330, 410 and 605 kcal/d. That stays inside ACSM and Murphy up to ~90 kg and inside AHA up to ~135 kg. Roth 2022 (systematic review) found that observed deficits in trained lifters averaged ~350-400 kcal/d, and case studies at ~580-882 kcal/d lost ~43% of weight as lean tissue. (3) Trials with good body-composition results achieved ~0.4-0.45%/wk (Conlin 2021; ICECAP, derived). (4) NASEM 2023 (moderate) cites a systematic review in which ~0.5 kg/wk preserved REE better than ~1.1 kg/wk. That supports the direction, not an exact rate. (5) Hall 2008: the static rule overstates the deficit needed when body fat is below ~30 kg, so lean users will probably lose faster than the target. The engine intervenes only beyond maxWeeklyLossFraction, so a lower target leaves more margin.

What this gives up: Garthe 2011, one RCT in elite athletes of both sexes (4 RT sessions/wk), is the basis of ACSM's EAL Q1 (Grade II, Fair). The slow arm (target 0.7%/wk) lost 0.7 +/- 0.8%/wk on a ~19% intake cut and gained lean mass (+2.1%). The fast arm (target 1.4%/wk) actually lost 1.0 +/- 0.4%/wk on a ~30% cut and kept lean mass flat (-0.2%). The slow arm took ~8.5 weeks instead of 5.3 to reach the same total loss. No trial compared 0.5 with 0.7%/wk. The owner may offer -0.007 as an opt-in for lean trained users; it is still inside maxWeeklyLossFraction.

Limits: the evidence comes from lean trained adults, and no source gives a body-fat cut-off for changing the rate (open gap). Obesity guidance gives kcal deficits instead (AHA 500-750; NICE trials 500-800), and no verified absolute kg/wk cap exists (open gallstone gap). So the safety-group energy floors still bind at high body mass.

Gating (safety group, not this value): the engine's safety_block withholds targets for pregnancy (IOM 2009 prescribes weight gain), lactation, SCOFF >=2 (refer) and listed conditions such as NICE's flags (e.g. type 1 diabetes), but only when safety.exclusions lists them. No engine gate stops fatLoss at low BMI. The owner should add one at BMI <18.5 (Triad 2014 restoration target; <=17.5 is the LEA flag). Lactation and glucose-lowering or GLP-1 drugs have no verified finding (open gaps), so exclude those users until reviewed. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #244, #245, #220, #227, #195, #345, #217, #218, #194, #346, #240, #231, #232, #780, #768, #54, #316, #723, #525, #472, #457, #479, #748, #740, #770, #366.

maxWeeklyLossFraction.locator: ACSM/AND/DC 2016 joint position statement, MSSE 48(3): p.548 'Principles of altering body composition and weight' ('<1% body mass per week'); Table 1 EAL Q1 p.544. Supporting trial: Garthe 2011, IJSNEM 21(2):97, PubMed abstract Results.
maxWeeklyLossFraction.note:
Unit: positive magnitude, as a fraction of body mass per week (0.01 = 1%/wk). weeklyChangeFraction is the signed target (-0.005). The engine never targets this rate. It compares the signed observed trend with -0.01, and a trend below that (losing faster than 1%/wk) triggers LOSING_FASTER_THAN_SAFE, a proposal to eat more. The comparison is strict, so a trend of exactly -1.0%/wk sits on the boundary and is not flagged.

Basis: ACSM 2016 says weekly loss should stay below 1% of body mass to protect fat-free mass and performance. Garthe 2011, the RCT behind it, supports putting the edge here: the fast arm (planned 1.4%/wk) actually lost 1.0 +/- 0.4%/wk and kept lean mass flat (-0.2%), while the 0.7%/wk arm gained it (+2.1%). In the Ruiz-Castellano case studies, about 43% of the weight lost at 1%/wk was fat-free mass.

This is the strictest cap stated as % of body mass. Helms 2014 and Ruiz-Castellano 2021 put 1%/wk at the top of their ranges. The Female Athlete Triad Coalition 2014 scores 5 to <10% loss in one month as moderate risk (about 1.2-2.3%/wk). It and IOC 2018 flag >=10% in a month as high risk or an LEA indicator. 1%/wk for a month (~4.3%) stays under the Triad's 5%/month band.

Once kcal sources are converted, it is not the tightest limit (my arithmetic, static 7,700 kcal/kg rule). 1%/wk is about 825 kcal/d at 75 kg and 1,100 at 100 kg. That is above ACSM's own 250-500 kcal/d, Murphy & Koehler 2022's ~500 kcal/d (abstract only) and AHA 2013's 500-750 kcal/d. Hall 2008 notes that the rule overstates the deficit when body fat is below ~30 kg. Observed losses of 0.5-1.0%/wk therefore go unflagged. The kcal limits are enforced through the target (weeklyChangeFraction) and the safety-group floors (e.g. safety.maximumDeficitFractionOfTEE, safety.minimumEnergyKcal), not through this cap.

Noise (my arithmetic; ~1% independent per-reading SD and a 28-day least-squares window assumed): the gap between target and cap is 0.005/wk. The slope SE is ~0.0016/wk with daily weigh-ins and ~0.0028/wk with 2.5 weigh-ins per week. A user exactly on target is therefore flagged in about 0.1% (daily) to 3.5% (2.5/wk) of checks, against 3-14% at the draft's -0.007 target. A false flag points toward eating more, the safe direction, and is only a proposal.

Caveats: (1) the evidence comes from athletes. (2) No verified finding gives an absolute kg/week cap for users with obesity. Johansson 2014 (Int J Obes 38(2):279-84; epub 2013) links larger early loss to gallstones but reports no threshold (open safety gap), so this fraction does not replace an absolute cap. Graded low: ACSM gives the cap without a pooled dose-response. NASEM 2023 (moderate) supports only the direction. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #195, #345, #217, #220, #244, #245, #474, #456, #54, #792, #194, #346, #240, #780, #525.

proteinGPerKgBodyMass.locator: ACSM/AND/DC 2016 joint position statement, MSSE 48(3): p.551 'Protein needs'; p.548 weight-loss paragraph; p.562 summary (DC concurrent publication p.17, p.11, p.36).
proteinGPerKgBodyMass.note:
Unit: g protein per kg body mass per day. ACSM gives >=2.0 g/kg/d during energy restriction, spread over the day. The value sits at that floor, the conservative choice among conflicting sources (a listed contradiction). The other sources: IAAF 2019 gives >1.6-2.4 g/kg BW. Ruiz-Castellano 2021 gives 2.2-3.0 g/kg BW. ISSN 2017 gives 2.3-3.1 'g/kg' with no cited source. Helms 2014 (a systematic review and a narrative review) gives 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM. That is about 1.7-2.6 g/kg body mass at 15-25% body fat (my arithmetic), so 2.0 fits its lower end. Trials used 1.8-2.4 g/kg BM: Campbell 2020 1.8, Conlin 2021 2.0, ICECAP 2.3, and Longland 2016 2.4 vs 1.2, where the higher dose gained more lean mass. IAAF 2019 says >2.5 g/kg/d adds no adaptation.

Cross-group: after any pattern multiplier, the engine clamps every goal's protein between macros.proteinMinimumGPerKgBodyMass and macros.proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass. That maximum must be at least 2.0, or this target is silently cut, and it should not exceed 2.5 (IAAF). Once BMI reaches macros.proteinReferenceFromBMI, the engine applies this per-kg value to a reference mass (macros.proteinReferenceBMI x height squared). The high-BMI denominator decision therefore sits in the macros group, not here. That group should keep absolute intakes near the kidney data below (~1.8 g/kg at ~92 kg, about 170 g/d). On actual mass, 2.0 g/kg at 120 kg would be ~240 g/d. The only overweight-specific figure is 1.2-1.5 g/kg, and it is second-hand (Martinez-Gomez & Roberts, JSCR 2022, narrative review).

Kidney: the Devries 2018 meta-analysis found no GFR difference with higher protein, including during energy restriction (low/very-low certainty). Higher-protein arms averaged 1.81 +/- 0.60 g/kg/d. Participants were adults without CKD, including people with obesity, T2D or hypertension: mean BMI 31.1, mean body mass 92.4 kg, study range 64.5-106.0 kg (checked in the full text). IAAF says 2.4 g/kg/d during weight loss is not linked to kidney or bone problems in healthy athletes.

Exclusion: users with clinician-diagnosed kidney disease, reduced eGFR, albuminuria or a kidney transplant get no automated protein target and are referred. KDIGO 2024 defines CKD as GFR <60 or ACR >=30 mg/g for >=3 months. It advises avoiding >1.3 g/kg/d in CKD at risk of progression and suggests 0.8 g/kg/d in G3-G5 (grade 2C). Undiagnosed CKD cannot be screened out, which is one more reason to stay at the ACSM floor. The evidence comes mainly from lean, resistance-trained adults. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #197, #341, #406, #162, #221, #250, #140, #166, #725, #317, #326, #407, #187, #189, #408, #565, #566, #388, #742, #743, #744.

weeklyChangeFraction.locator: Iraki J et al. 2019, Sports (Basel) 7(7):154: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance'; Section 8 Summary; Abstract.
weeklyChangeFraction.note: Unit: signed fraction of body mass per week (+0.0025 = gain 0.25%/wk). No objection; kept as drafted, with wording aligned to the maxWeeklyGainFraction correction. Iraki 2019 recommends about 0.25-0.5% of body mass per week for novice and intermediate lifters, and slower for advanced lifters. It is a narrative review, so this cannot be graded above low. It is the only verified source that gives a %BW/wk gain rate. The default is the lower bound because the extra gain from a larger surplus was mostly fat. In Garthe 2013 (elite athletes), a counselled surplus of about 0.3-0.5%/wk (derived, not reported) raised fat mass by 15% against 3% with ad libitum eating, and lean-mass gain did not differ. Iraki describes the trial as +1.7 kg lean and +1.1 kg fat vs +1.2 kg and +0.2 kg. In Ribeiro 2019 (a pilot), the higher intake added significant fat for little extra estimated muscle. Iraki also cites a trial suggesting 200-300 kcal/d for highly trained athletes. Slater 2019 states that the optimal surplus has not been established. Gaps: no verified trial compares gain rates, and no finding separates novices from advanced lifters or men from women. Cross-group: stableBandFractionPerWeek is derived as half of this value, so re-derive the band if this changes. The gap to maxWeeklyGainFraction is 0.0025/wk. With a 28-day window and ~1% per-reading SD (my arithmetic), a user exactly on target would be flagged GAINING_FASTER_THAN_GOAL in about 6% (daily weigh-ins) to 18% (2.5/wk) of checks. A false flag only proposes eating slightly less. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #259, #258, #262, #294, #287, #260, #272, #271, #275.

maxWeeklyGainFraction.locator: Iraki J et al. 2019, Sports (Basel) 7(7):154: Section 2 Energy, 'Positive Energy Balance'; Section 8 Summary; Abstract.
maxWeeklyGainFraction.note: Unit: positive fraction of body mass per week (0.005 = 0.5%/wk). The engine flags GAINING_FASTER_THAN_GOAL, a proposal to eat less, only when the observed trend is strictly above this value. It is a ceiling, not a target. 0.5%/wk is the top of the Iraki 2019 range, which applies to novice and intermediate lifters; advanced lifters should gain more slowly. Garthe 2013 (elite athletes, mean age about 19 y) shows the cost of gaining near this band. The counselled group gained about 0.3-0.5%/wk (derived: +3.9% over 8-12 wk), and the ad libitum group about 0.1-0.2%/wk (+1.5%). Fat mass rose 15% vs 3%, and lean-mass gain did not differ. Iraki 2019 describes a matching trial (about 600 kcal/d over ad libitum): +1.7 kg lean and +1.1 kg fat vs +1.2 kg and +0.2 kg. So the extra gain over ad libitum was mostly fat, although the counselled group's total gain was not. Ribeiro 2019 (67.5 vs 50.1 kcal/kg/d) likewise added significant fat for little extra estimated muscle. The source is a narrative review, so this is graded low, and no trial has tested a gain-rate ceiling. Do not confuse this with the Triad 2014 weight-restoration pace (about 0.5 kg every 7-10 days). That is a treatment target for female athletes with low energy availability or amenorrhoea, not a muscle-gain cap. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #259, #294, #287, #258, #260, #477.

proteinGPerKgBodyMass.locator: Morton RW et al. 2018, Br J Sports Med 52(6):376: Results, 'Break point analysis'; Figure 5; Results 'Meta-analyses' and 'Meta-regression' (Table 1). Corroborated by Nunes EA et al. 2022, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, Table 2 and Results 'Effect of additional protein intake on lean body mass'.
proteinGPerKgBodyMass.note:
Unit: g protein per kg body mass per day. Two meta-analyses agree.

Morton 2018 pooled 49 RCTs of healthy adults doing resistance training for >=6 weeks, trained and untrained, none energy-restricted (mean age 35 y). It put the plateau for training-induced FFM gain at 1.62 g/kg/d. The estimate is imprecise (95% CI 1.03-2.20), and the biphasic model did not reach significance (p = 0.079). Nunes 2022 (healthy, non-obese adults) found a significant lean-mass gain only at >=1.6 g/kg/d in under-65s (SMD 0.30, moderate GRADE); 1.2-1.59 g/kg/d was not significant. IOC 2018 calls 1.6 optimal, with no adverse effects up to 2.2.

Morton suggests about 2.2 g/kg/d (its upper CI) for users trying to maximise gain, and Iraki 2019 (narrative) also leans toward 2.2. That is a possible owner-set upper option, not the default, and it must stay within macros.proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass. The engine clamps to that value after any pattern multiplier, so the maximum must also be >=1.6.

The expected benefit is modest. Morton found about 0.3 kg extra FFM on top of the ~1.1 kg that training alone gave over ~13 weeks, and Nunes found 0.5-0.7 kg over 8-12 weeks. In Morton's training-status meta-regression (10 studies in trained participants), the effect was clear in resistance-trained participants (+1.05 kg FFM) and small and non-significant in untrained ones (+0.15 kg). Age: in Morton the benefit was clear under 45 y and not significant over 45 y. Nunes found no trial that tested >=1.6 g/kg/d in adults 65+. PROT-AGE sets >=1.2 g/kg/d for active older adults, which 1.6 already exceeds. The value applies only with resistance training: without it, extra protein did not increase lean mass (Nunes, low GRADE).

Kidney: Devries 2018 found no GFR difference in adults without CKD on higher-protein arms averaging 1.81 g/kg/d (low/very-low certainty). Users with clinician-diagnosed kidney disease, reduced eGFR, albuminuria or a kidney transplant (KDIGO 2024 definition) get no automated target and are referred. KDIGO advises avoiding >1.3 g/kg/d in CKD at risk of progression. At high BMI the engine applies this per-kg value to a reference mass once BMI reaches macros.proteinReferenceFromBMI, so that decision sits in the macros group. On actual mass, 1.6 x 120 kg would be 192 g/d. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #132, #133, #134, #135, #136, #137, #155, #156, #157, #158, #159, #386, #263, #279, #139, #196, #181, #187, #742, #744.

weeklyChangeFraction.locator: NASEM 2023, Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy: Summary pp.11-14; Ch. 7, pp.146-147 and 169.
weeklyChangeFraction.note: No objection; kept as drafted. By DRI definition, energy intake meets the requirement when body weight is stable. The DRI says to monitor weight and adjust intake step by step, so the maintenance target is zero change, and the engine adds no energy offset. FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 likewise sets energy at the average requirement with no margin. Zero also fits recomposition within maintenance: in Morton 2018, added protein with resistance training raised FFM (+0.30 kg) and lowered fat (-0.41 kg) with no significant change in total mass. Caveat (Triad 2014): a stable weight does not prove adequate energy availability, because chronic deficits can stabilise weight through physiological suppression. Low-EA screening must stay separate from this target. The engine judges the trend against stableBandFractionPerWeek, not against this value. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #50, #38, #135, #471.

proteinGPerKgBodyMass.locator: Morton RW et al. 2018, Br J Sports Med 52(6):376: Results, 'Break point analysis'; Figure 5 (population not energy-restricted). Nunes EA et al. 2022, Table 2.
proteinGPerKgBodyMass.note: Unit: g protein per kg body mass per day. No objection to the value. The note is aligned with the corrections accepted for the other protein targets: the Morton population, the KDIGO exclusion, and the high-BMI mass handled in the macros group. Morton's 1.62 g/kg/d break point comes from healthy adults doing resistance training, trained and untrained, who were not energy-restricted, a population that covers energy balance. Nunes 2022 found no significant added lean mass at 1.2-1.59 g/kg/d in under-65s, only at >=1.6. Other synthesis ranges that include 1.6: IAAF 2019 1.3-1.7 g/kg/d for weight-stable or gaining athletes; ISSN 2017 1.4-2.0; ACSM 2016 1.2-2.0. ACSM also says protein should follow energy availability and training rather than a goal label, which supports using the same value as muscleGain. The DRI RDA of 0.8 g/kg/d (IOM 2005; FAO/WHO 0.83) is only an adequacy floor, and Morton judged it insufficient for resistance-training goals. The value applies to users who do resistance training: without it, higher protein did not raise lean mass (Nunes, low GRADE). Kidney: Devries 2018 found no GFR difference in adults without CKD on higher-protein arms averaging 1.81 g/kg/d (low/very-low certainty). Users with clinician-diagnosed kidney disease, reduced eGFR, albuminuria or a kidney transplant (KDIGO 2024 definition) get no automated target and are referred. KDIGO advises avoiding >1.3 g/kg/d in CKD at risk of progression. Cross-group: macros.proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass must be >=1.6. At high BMI the engine applies this per-kg value to a reference mass once BMI reaches macros.proteinReferenceFromBMI, so that decision sits in the macros group. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #132, #134, #155, #405, #139, #196, #158, #62, #160, #181, #187, #742, #744.

stableBandFractionPerWeek.rationale: This is an owner choice derived from cited findings, not a value from the literature. (1) Noise floor: morning weight moves less than 1% from day to day in a person who is euhydrated and in energy balance (ACSM 2007, finding 489; ISSN 2019, about +/-1%, finding 434). NoHoW shows a systematic day-of-week cycle of about 0.35%, and detrended single readings spread about 1.0-1.2% (finding 589). People manage about 2.5-4 weigh-ins per week (finding 593). Fluid shifts can move short-term weight: Hall 2019 estimated 14-day change by linear regression to damp fluid fluctuations, and between-diet sodium differences tracked weight change (finding 819). So only a smoothed multi-week slope can carry a weekly drift band (NASEM: monitor over time and adjust, finding 50). (2) Separability: the slowest non-zero target in this bundle is muscleGain +0.25%/wk (Iraki 2019, finding 259; fatLoss is now -0.5%/wk). Placing the band edge midway between 0 and 0.0025 gives 0.00125, so a trend counts as stable exactly when it is closer to maintenance than to the slowest intended change. (3) Long-term check: drift at the band edge reaches Stevens' 3% long-term maintenance limit after 24 weeks, so the band cannot hide a clinically relevant drift over a half-year. The AHA 2013 regain of 1-2 kg/yr (finding 784; about 0.02-0.05%/wk at 80 kg) falls well inside the band and would count as stable, so a separate cumulative-drift check is advisable. (4) Resolvability (my arithmetic, assuming independent errors with SD about 1%): the least-squares slope SE is about 0.16%/wk for 4 weeks of daily weigh-ins and about 0.06%/wk for 8 weeks. A +/-0.125%/wk band is resolved reliably only with about 8 weeks of near-daily data or equivalent smoothing. The smoothing choices used in research (finding 592) are not a validated app rule. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #489, #434, #589, #593, #592, #50, #259, #784, #819.

weeklyChangeFraction.rationale: No verified source prescribes a weight-change rate for an endurance-performance goal, so this is an owner decision. (1) NASEM 2023 defines intake that keeps weight stable as meeting the energy requirement (finding 50, high). (2) ACSM 2016 advises scheduling planned loss in the base phase or well before competition, not during performance-focused training (finding 195). (3) IOC 2023 REDs describes about 45 kcal/kg FFM/day as adequate EA for weight maintenance, with 30-45 used for loss (finding 442, low). It counts only short, monitored body-composition phases as adaptable LEA, and treats prolonged deficits as problematic (finding 446). Thresholds in men appear lower but are uncertain (finding 443). Defaulting endurance users to energy balance avoids an unrequested deficit on top of high training expenditure. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #50, #195, #442, #446, #471, #55, #443.

proteinGPerKgBodyMass.rationale: The syntheses give only ranges, and they conflict (a listed contradiction): ACSM 2016 1.2-2.0 g/kg/d (findings 196, 341); IAAF 2019 1.3-1.7 for weight-stable athletes (finding 405); ISSN ultra-marathon 2019 1.6-2.1, up to 2.5 in demanding training, with a warning that nitrogen balance may turn negative below 1.6 in high-volume athletes (finding 424); T1D exercise consensus 2017 1.2-1.6, drawn from athletes without diabetes (finding 760); ISSN protein 2017 1.4-2.0 (finding 139). 1.6 g/kg/d is the only value inside every one of these ranges. It is also the ISSN ultra floor below which negative nitrogen balance is flagged. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #196, #405, #424, #760, #139, #341, #754, #187, #742, #744.

carbohydrateGPerKgByTrainingLoad.locator: ACSM/AND/DC 2016 joint position statement, MSSE 48(3): p.550 Table 2 'Daily needs for fuel and recovery' (adapted from Burke et al. 2011); p.562 summary (DC concurrent publication Table 1 p.15, Summary p.36).
carbohydrateGPerKgByTrainingLoad.note: Unit: g carbohydrate per kg body mass per day. No objection; kept as drafted. The engine uses each band's midpoint (4, 6, 8 and 10 g/kg/d) for the user-selected load and raises energy if fat would fall below its minimum share. Load definitions (ACSM Table 2): light = low-intensity or skill-based activities; moderate = a moderate exercise programme, about 1 h/day; high = an endurance programme, 1-3 h/day of moderate-to-high-intensity exercise; veryHigh = extreme commitment, >4-5 h/day of moderate-to-high-intensity exercise. Caveats: (1) The bands overlap (high 6-10 vs veryHigh 8-12), and about 3-4 h/day is not defined, so the engine needs an owner rule for users there. (2) ACSM says the targets apply when session quality or intensity matters. They should be periodised day to day, and on other days intake may follow energy goals or be lowered on purpose. (3) Consistent sources: ISSN nutrient timing 2017 (5-12 g/kg/d; 8-10 or 8-12 for high volume, with internally inconsistent hour cut-offs), ISSN ultra 2019 (5-8 for 2-3 h/day, 7-10 for greater volume), and the ISSN 2017 protein stand citing 6-10. (4) Endurance goal only: Henselmans 2022 found no carbohydrate minimum for strength-training performance. (5) For typical adult body masses, every band's lower bound is above the IOM carbohydrate RDA of 130 g/d. This is not an AMDR (45-65% energy) check. (6) The statement lists itself as in effect until 31 Dec 2019; no newer ACSM table was verified. (7) Users with type 1 diabetes are excluded from automated fuelling targets. Graded low per the verified finding: it is a consensus table without graded evidence, though several independent position stands agree. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #200, #336, #368, #423, #150, #330, #754, #64, #68.

fatMinimumEnergyFraction.locator: IOM 2005 DRI Macronutrients, Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332), AMDR table, total fat, row '19 years and over': 20-35% of energy (finding 65). Checked against the same AMDR table in the Health Canada DRI reproduction. Supported by ACSM 2016, 'Fat', MSSE p.552 (finding 343; same text in the DC co-publication pp.18-19, finding 207).
fatMinimumEnergyFraction.note: Revised on review: I accepted both objections. The value is unchanged; only the wording and locator were fixed. The sources conflict. The IOM adult AMDR (65) and ACSM 2016 (207, 343) both put the floor at 20%. ACSM discourages chronic intake below 20%. It says intakes at or below 20% give no performance benefit and risk shortfalls of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids (343). So 0.20 is the inclusive lower edge of the AMDR, not a target. In diet.macros_for, fat starts at the 0.25 default. It reaches 0.20 only when carbohydrate squeezes energy: the 130 g floor, or the training-load carbohydrate in the endurance path. Slater 2019 (282) discourages going below 15-20%. Helms 2014 (222) accepts 15-20% during a cut, and Martinez-Gomez & Roberts 2022 (569) allow 10-25%. Both are narrative reviews of lean athletes or dieters. I chose the conservative 20% because this floor is safety-related. ACSM ties it to fatty-acid and fat-soluble-vitamin adequacy, and Ruiz-Castellano 2021 (257) links fat at or below 20% with lower testosterone. This fraction does not cover the gram-based checks, which belong in separate parameters: (a) the essential fatty acid AIs (67): linoleic acid 17 g (men) and 12 g (women) at 19-50 y, 14 and 11 g at 51+ y, and alpha-linolenic acid 1.6 and 1.1 g at 19+ y; (b) at least 0.5 g/kg (257); (c) the 7-10 g/d gallbladder-emptying threshold cited by Johansson 2013 (793). These gram checks bind at low energy. At about 1,200 kcal (the female energy floor in the safety group's draft), 0.20 gives about 27 g fat/d, which is below 0.5 g/kg for anyone heavier than about 53 kg. Age 18: the DRI AMDR table has no 14-18 y row. 18-year-olds fall in its '4-18 years' row, where fat is 25-35% (Health Canada DRI reproduction, AMDR table). With safety.minimumAgeYears drafted at 19, every user is in the '19 years and over' row. This matters only if the owner lowers the minimum age to 18, and the owner would then decide whether to apply 0.25 at 18. The IOM full text was not opened, so this value comes from the Summary Tables. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #65, #207, #343, #282, #222, #569, #257, #67, #793.

fatMaximumEnergyFraction.locator: IOM 2005 DRI Macronutrients, Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332), AMDR table, total fat, row '19 years and over': upper bound 35% of energy (finding 65). Same upper bound in ACSM 2016, 'Fat', MSSE p.552 (finding 343; DC co-publication pp.18-19, finding 207).
fatMaximumEnergyFraction.note: Revised on review: I accepted both objections. The value is unchanged; I fixed the locator and the age-row wording and added an engine caveat. This is the IOM AMDR upper bound (65). ACSM 2016 (207, 343), Slater 2019 (282), Iraki 2019 (267) and the exercise consensus for athletes with type 1 diabetes (762) all use the same 35%. The AMDR is population-level guidance on chronic-disease risk, not a toxicity limit; total fat has no UL (65). AHA 2013 (788) compared diets at a 500-750 kcal/d deficit. Diets above 40% fat gave the same 6-12-month weight loss as diets below 30%, so a higher ceiling has not been shown to harm weight loss. Still, no official source sets a ceiling above 35%, so I kept the conservative value. As a result the app never generates ketogenic or high-fat targets. That fits the performance cautions from ISSN (ultra-marathon, 437) and IAAF (fat adaptation impairs performance above about 80-85% VO2peak, 415). Age: the DRI AMDR row that would cover 18-year-olds is '4-18 years' (there is no 14-18 y row). It has the same 35% upper bound (Health Canada DRI reproduction, AMDR table). So the value holds whether safety.minimumAgeYears stays at the drafted 19 or is lowered to 18. Engine issue (does not change this value): in the endurance training-load path, diet.macros_for caps fat at this fraction (fat = min(fat, fat_maximum)). It does not give the removed energy to carbohydrate or lower energyKcal. So when the cap binds, the macro grams add up to less than energyKcal. The engine should reassign that energy or recompute energy. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #65, #207, #343, #282, #267, #762, #788, #437, #415.

fatDefaultEnergyFraction.rationale: Several findings point to 0.25. (1) It sits inside the IOM adult AMDR of 20-35% (65), 5 percentage points above the 20% floor that ACSM discourages going below (207, 343). Ordinary logging slippage therefore does not drop users below the floor. (2) With safety.minimumAgeYears drafted at 19, every user falls in the DRI '19 years and over' AMDR row (20-35%). If the owner lowers the minimum age to 18, 0.25 is also the lower bound of the DRI '4-18 years' fat AMDR (25-35%; Health Canada DRI reproduction, AMDR table), so the default would still suit 18-year-olds. (3) It is the midpoint of Ruiz-Castellano's 20-30% 'where feasible' (257) and of the Nordic 20-30% protocol range used by Martins 2020 (582). It matches the 25% fat in the ISSN 60/15/25 split for ultra-endurance training (426) and the lower end of MATADOR's planned 25-30% (313). Peos 2021 used about 20% (318). (4) A lower-middle default leaves most non-protein energy for carbohydrate. Helms 2014 (222, 223) and Ruiz-Castellano 2021 (257) prioritise carbohydrate over extra fat for training. Iraki 2019 says fat should not crowd out protein or carbohydrate (267) and aims carbohydrate at 3-5 g/kg/d or more (268). WHO 2023 (797) says carbohydrate should follow from the protein and fat targets. (5) AHA 2013 (788) shows that fat share does not change weight loss at a matched deficit. The default is therefore a choice about training fuel and adequacy, not about fat-loss efficacy. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #65, #207, #343, #257, #582, #426, #313, #318, #222, #223, #267, #268, #797, #788.

carbohydrateMinimumGPerDay.locator: IOM 2005 DRI Macronutrients, Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332), macronutrient reference-value table, carbohydrate: EAR 100 g/d, RDA 130 g/d, adults 19+ y, non-pregnant (finding 68)
carbohydrateMinimumGPerDay.note: No objection was raised. The value is kept, and I updated only the priority-order sentence to match diet.macros_for. This is an adequacy floor (the RDA), not a training or performance intake. ACSM's g/kg/d targets by training load (200, 336) are separate. The sources conflict: (a) the IOM EAR is 100 g/d (68); (b) EFSA sets a 30 g/d minimum for total diet replacements (776, abstract only); (c) AHA 2013 accepted a low-carbohydrate diet of about 20 g/d for weight loss (789); (d) Henselmans 2022 found no carbohydrate minimum for strength (330). On the cautious side, Ruiz-Castellano 2021 warns that ketogenic intakes may preserve less fat-free mass (255). IOC REDs 2023 links intakes below 3 g/kg/d with worse bone, immune and iron markers in endurance athletes (444). I chose the conservative RDA, so the app will not generate low-carbohydrate or ketogenic targets. This does not claim that lower intakes are unsafe. The DRI table gives the same 130 g/d for the 14-18 y group, so the value holds if the owner lowers safety.minimumAgeYears to 18. diet.macros_for sets the priority order outside the endurance training-load path: protein first, fat at the 0.25 default, carbohydrate as the remainder. If carbohydrate falls below 130 g, fat drops toward the 0.20 minimum. If that is still short, carbohydrate is held at 130 g and energy is raised (ENERGY_RAISED_FOR_CARBOHYDRATE_FLOOR). In the endurance path, carbohydrate is max(130 g, training-load g/kg x body mass). Pregnancy and lactation values differ, but those users are excluded. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #68, #776, #789, #330, #255, #444, #200, #336.

proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass.locator: Morton et al. 2018, Br J Sports Med, Discussion 'Muscle mass', paragraph on the two-segment regression: about 2.2 g/kg/d, the upper 95% CI bound of the 1.62 g/kg/d break point (finding 133; Results 'Break point analysis' and Figure 5, finding 132). Supported by the IOC 2018 dietary supplements consensus, Table 6 (Gaining LBM, Protein row): up to 2.2 g/kg/d with no adverse effects (finding 386).
proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass.note:
Revised on review. I accepted the objection that moves the ceiling from 2.4 to 2.2, and the wording fixes from the other objection (the ISSN and Helms ranges, and the Longland result). The candidate ceilings conflict. Because this is the safety ceiling, I chose the most conservative value a synthesis supports, as the task rule for safety-related conflicts requires.
- Morton 2018 (meta-analysis): about 2.2 g/kg/d, the upper 95% CI bound of the 1.62 break point (133). The break point's CI was 1.03-2.20 across tested intakes of 0.9-2.4 (132). This is a benefit estimate: no added FFM gain is shown above it.
- IOC 2018: up to 2.2 with no adverse effects (386).
- IAAF 2019: more than 1.6 and up to 2.4 during weight loss with resistance exercise (406). Above 2.5 gives no adaptive advantage (407). About 2.4 during weight loss is not associated with kidney or bone risk in healthy athletes (408).
- ACSM 2016: at least 2.0 during restriction (197).
- Higher ranges: ISSN 2017 prints 2.3-3.1 per kg body weight with no source cited (140). The Helms 2014 systematic review gives 2.3-3.1 per kg FFM in lean lifters (162). Ruiz-Castellano 2021 (narrative review) gives 2.2-3.0 per kg body weight (250). So 2.2 is not the only synthesis-backed ceiling, and it deliberately cuts off these higher ranges.
Safety reasoning:
- The Devries 2018 kidney meta-analysis found no dose threshold. But its higher-protein arms averaged 1.81 +/- 0.60 g/kg (participants' mean BMI 31.1), so its data do not show safety far above that range (187, 188). 2.2 is closer to the tested range than 2.4.
- Slater 2019 says long-term safety above about 2.5 g/kg is not validated (280).
- The app can exclude only users who report CKD. KDIGO advises avoiding more than 1.3 g/kg in CKD at risk of progression (742; CKD definition, 744). KDIGO 2024 also states that only 6% of the general population and 10% of the high-risk population know their CKD status (Introduction, 'Screening and prevention', p.S138). I confirmed this in the guideline text; it is not yet a finding record.
- Both 2.2 and 2.4 exceed 1.3, so the CKD point supports a lower ceiling and a screen, not a specific number. The owner should consider asking users who report diabetes, hypertension or CVD to confirm their kidney function with a clinician before giving targets above 1.3 g/kg. No finding tests such a screen.
Effect on goals:
- The ceiling clips any goal target above 2.2. That includes the top of the IAAF range and the 2.4 arm of Longland 2016, a single RCT. In a deficit of about 40%, 2.4 vs 1.2 g/kg/d gave more lean-mass gain there (+1.2 vs +0.1 kg; 166, abstract only).
- 2.2 still meets ACSM's 2.0 or more during restriction (197) and sits inside IAAF's 1.6-2.4 (406).
- For a user at about 15% body fat, 2.2 g/kg body mass equals 2.59 g/kg FFM, inside Helms's 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM (162).
- If the owner accepts the extra exposure, 2.4 (IAAF 2019, fat loss only; findings 406-408) is the cited alternative.
Engine:
- The ceiling applies to the mass chosen by proteinBodyMassRule.
- The engine should also cap protein at the IOM adult protein AMDR upper bound of 35% of energy (63); diet.macros_for does not check this today. At 2.2 g/kg, a 70 kg user passes 35% below about 1,760 kcal/d.
- If the owner lowers safety.minimumAgeYears to 18, the DRI '4-18 years' AMDR row caps protein at 30% (Health Canada DRI reproduction, AMDR table).
- The ceiling does not apply to CKD (742); those users are excluded. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #133, #132, #386, #406, #407, #408, #197, #166, #187, #188, #280, #63, #742, #744, #140, #250, #162.

proteinMinimumGPerKgBodyMass.locator: IOM 2005 DRI Macronutrients, Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332), 'Reference Values for Macronutrients' table, total protein RDA: 0.85 g/kg/d for males and females 14-18 y and 0.80 g/kg/d for 19+ y (the adult value is finding 62; Ch. 10 pp.589-768). The 14-18 y value was read in the Health Canada reproduction of the DRI summary tables (macronutrient table and footnote 30), not in the IOM full text.
proteinMinimumGPerKgBodyMass.note:
Revised on review. I accepted the objection that raises the floor to 0.85, and the wording fixes from the objection that kept 0.8. The age-18 point is conditional on the minimum age, and the reference-weight BMI and the EFSA height cut-off are now exact. This is an adequacy floor only, and the sources conflict:
- The IOM RDA is 0.80 g/kg/d for ages 19 and over (62).
- FAO/WHO and EFSA give 0.83, restated in Nunes 2022 (160); their primary reports were not opened.
- The IOM RDA for 14-18 y is 0.85 (DRI summary macronutrient table, read in the Health Canada reproduction).
A higher floor has no safety downside, so I chose the most conservative value, 0.85, as the task rule asks for safety-related conflicts. It covers the FAO/WHO/EFSA figure for adults. It would also cover 18-year-olds if the owner lowers safety.minimumAgeYears from the drafted 19 to 18, because the DRI puts 18-year-olds in the 14-18 y group. With the minimum age at 19, the extra 0.05 g/kg over the adult RDA (3.5 g/d at 70 kg) is below food-logging precision. If the owner prefers the exact adult RDA, 0.80 (62) is the cited alternative. The fat floor is handled differently: its 4-18 y value (25%) is not applied to adults. Raising a protein floor that does not bind costs nothing, while raising the fat floor to 0.25 would remove the room the engine uses when energy is squeezed.
The floor is far below resistance-training needs. Morton 2018 judged the RDA insufficient (134), and Nunes 2022 found lean-mass gains only at 1.6 g/kg/d or more (155). In diet.protein_target the floor binds only if a goal target times a pattern multiplier falls below 0.85. So it guards against future owner changes rather than shaping today's targets.
The DRI computes gram values for everyone as the per-kg value times a reference weight (62; DRI table footnote 30). Those weights, 70 kg at 1.77 m and 57 kg at 1.63 m, sit at BMI about 22.3 and 21.5 (Health Canada reproduction). proteinBodyMassRule borrows this precedent, but it uses measured mass below BMI 30 and a BMI-25 reference mass only at 30 and above.
EFSA sets a 75 g/d protein minimum for total diet replacements in adults with overweight or obesity (775, abstract only). For heights below about 1.88 m, 75 g/d is more than 0.85 x the BMI-25 reference mass, so a severe-deficit mode would need its own absolute floor. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #62, #160, #134, #155, #775.

fibreGPer1000Kcal.locator: IOM 2005 DRI Macronutrients, Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332), total fiber AI with footnote 32: AI based on 14 g/1,000 kcal x median usual energy intake; men 38 / women 25 g/d at 19-50 y (finding 69). Footnotes 31-32 checked in the Health Canada DRI reproduction.
fibreGPer1000Kcal.note: Revised on review: I accepted both objections. The value is unchanged. I corrected the pre-event and definition citations and added a high-energy cap caveat. This is an Adequate Intake, not an RDA. The DRI's own gram values are 14 g/1,000 kcal x median usual energy intake (69; DRI table footnote 32), so scaling to the user's calorie target follows the DRI derivation. The 14-18 y values (boys 38, girls 26 g/d) use the same basis. Low end: below about 1,790 kcal the result is under 25 g/d. That is below WHO 2023's minimum of 25 g/d of naturally occurring fibre (796, strong recommendation) and below the 25-29 g/d supported by the Reynolds 2019 meta-analyses (801). The engine should therefore also apply that absolute floor as a separate parameter. High end: above about 2,860 kcal the result exceeds 40 g/d, the top of the range over which WHO saw benefit rise (796). Targets of 3,500-4,300 kcal give about 49-60 g/d. The dose-response shows no plateau within the observed data (802), and no fibre-related harms were found (808), apart from a qualitative caution for marginal iron status. But no benefit or harm was observed beyond that range. IOC RED-S 2018 (461) lists high fibre among diet traits that can compound low energy availability. The users with the highest energy targets are high-volume trainees and surplus users. The engine should therefore cap the scaled target: 40 g/d, the top of the WHO range, is the suggested cap, as an owner decision in a separate parameter. ACSM 2016 (338) and IAAF 2019 (411) advise low-fibre pre-event meals to limit gut upset. So the target should not be pushed during low energy availability or before events. Definitions differ. IOM total fibre is dietary plus functional (isolated) fibre (DRI table footnote 31). WHO counts only naturally occurring fibre (798). Meat-eaters most often fall short of the fibre AI: about 21 g/d vs 28 for vegetarians and 44 for vegans (691). Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #69, #796, #801, #802, #808, #798, #461, #338, #411, #691.

proteinReferenceFromBMI.rationale:
(1) The g/kg evidence was built on measured mass in non-obese or lean samples. Nunes 2022 excluded participants with obesity and weight-loss protocols (155, 157; Methods and Table 1 exclusion criteria). Morton 2018 studied healthy adults (132). Helms 2014 included lean samples only: men <=23% and women <=35% body fat (164). That supports measured mass below BMI 30.
(2) There is official precedent for a healthy-weight denominator, but no official rule for obesity. The DRI computes the protein RDA in grams for every adult as the per-kg value multiplied by a reference weight, giving 56 and 46 g/d (62; DRI table footnote 30, 'per kg body weight multiplied by the reference weight'). Those reference weights sit at BMI about 22.3 and 21.5 (Health Canada reproduction). FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 sets the healthy individual range at BMI 18.5-24.9 (39). BMI 25, the rounded upper bound of that range, is therefore the most generous healthy-weight mass, heavier than the DRI reference person. That keeps targets for muscular users closer to the lean-sample evidence. Using measured mass below BMI 30 and switching only at 30 is the owner's choice.
(3) Check against the only obesity figure. Martinez-Gomez & Roberts 2022 cite 1.2-1.5 g/kg for adults with overweight or obesity in a deficit (565, a secondary citation). In g/kg of measured mass at BMI 30, 35 and 40, the rule gives:
- 2.2 ceiling: 1.83, 1.57 and 1.375 (inside 1.2-1.5 only from about BMI 37);
- 2.0 target: 1.67, 1.43 and 1.25 (inside from about BMI 33);
- 1.6 target: 1.33, 1.14 and 1.00 (inside only up to about BMI 33, below it above that).
So the rule does not reproduce the 1.2-1.5 figure. High targets sit above it at the low end of the obese range, and 1.6 targets fall below it at higher BMI. Even so, 1.6 targets stay above the 0.8 g/kg adult RDA on measured mass up to BMI 50. The ceiling-derived values lie within about one SD of the higher-protein arms (1.81 +/- 0.60 g/kg) of the Devries 2018 kidney meta-analysis, whose participants had BMI 21.2-36.1, mean 31.1 (187). The owner should confirm this band, or choose a different reference BMI, once the two unopened sources are checked.
(4) Further precedent for a healthy-weight denominator: PROT-AGE sets its severe-CKD protein limit per kg of ideal body weight (184). EFSA adjusts the protein reference intake for adults with overweight or obesity rather than using it unchanged (775, abstract only; method not verified). Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #155, #157, #132, #164, #62, #39, #565, #187, #184, #775.
