proteinMaximumEnergyFraction.locator: Summary and Summary Tables (pp.1319-1332); cited pp.12, 15 and p.1325 not verified
proteinMaximumEnergyFraction.note: IOM 2005 adult protein AMDR: 10-35% of energy; no UL for protein. The engine caps protein at 35% of the energy target, as the review of macros.proteinMaximumGPerKgBodyMass asked. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #63.

fibreMinimumG.locator: Recommendation 4 and rationale (printed pp.22, 24-25); Table 2 and Review 1 in Summary of evidence (printed pp.9, 13)
fibreMinimumG.note: WHO 2023: at least 25 g/day of naturally occurring fibre for adults (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence). The displayed fibre target is max(25 g, 14 g per 1,000 kcal), capped at fibreMaximumG. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #796.

fibreMaximumG.rationale: The fibre target is cited; its cap and its role in ranking are owner rules. WHO 2023 advises at least 25 g/day of naturally occurring fibre for adults (finding 796: strong recommendation, moderate certainty). IOM 2005 sets the total-fibre AI at 14 g per 1,000 kcal (finding 69, graded moderate, but its pages were not verified). For every goal the daily target is the larger of the two, so it scales with the user's energy target and never falls below the WHO floor. It is the same number as the fibreG target the engine displays (macros.fibreGPer1000Kcal = 14), so the app has one fibre target. The target is capped at 40 g/day, the top of the dose-response range in the WHO evidence (finding 796). Reynolds 2019 found a linear dose-response with no plateau, but only within the observed data (findings 801-802), so no benefit is shown above about 40 g. Harms at high intakes are plausible for some users: IOC 2018 lists high fibre intake and low-energy-density foods among diet traits that can compound low energy availability (finding 461); a sports-nutrition review warns that very high intakes could impair absorption of some nutrients (finding 256); and very large whole-grain intakes may worsen marginal iron status (finding 808). The cap binds above about 2,860 kcal/day and stays above every IOM gram AI (the highest is 38 g/day, men 19-50; finding 69). Reynolds' broadest benefit at 25-29 g/day and its linear slope support a ranking bonus while intake is below target. For fatLoss and maintenance the bonus runs up to the daily target. For muscleGain and endurance it stops at the 25 g WHO floor even when the displayed target is higher. The reason is energy density, not a fibre-satiety effect, which the app does not claim because interventional satiety evidence is inconsistent (finding 574). Fibre-rich whole foods are low in energy density (finding 834), lowering energy density cut ad libitum intake in feeding studies (finding 827), and raising energy density is the advised lever when appetite limits a surplus, while keeping vegetables at public-health levels (finding 285). For endurance, IOC 2018 names high fibre and low-energy-density foods as possible compounders of low energy availability (finding 461), and pre-race and during-exercise foods should be low in fibre (findings 411, 432, 383). Because the displayed target still scales for these goals and nothing penalises higher intake, the IOM-based target is still shown. Only intrinsic fibre counts: WHO counts only fibre naturally present in foods (finding 798), and Reynolds favours minimally processed sources (finding 807). The IOM AI is for total fibre (finding 69), so counting only intrinsic fibre against it is at least as strict as IOM. Fibre is only a tie-breaker because its effect on body weight is small (-0.37 kg in RCTs that excluded weight-loss trials, finding 803). Applying the iron caution (finding 808) to plant-based users, who already average 28-44 g/day (finding 691), is our inference, not the authors'. WHO ranks whole grains, vegetables, fruit and pulses first as carbohydrate sources (finding 794), and whole grains outperform refined grains in cohort data (finding 804, low GRADE); ranking by fibre per 100 kcal reproduces both. Fibre-free foods get no penalty, since a penalty would push protein foods down the ranking. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #796, #69, #798, #800, #801, #802, #803, #804, #805, #807, #808, #461, #256, #574, #285, #794, #691, #827, #834, #411, #432, #383.

trendMethod.locator: Hall KD et al. 2019, Cell Metab 30(1):67-77, full text (PMC): STAR Methods 'Body weight and composition' (14-day weight change estimated by linear regression of daily 06:00 post-void weights to damp body-fluid fluctuations)
trendMethod.note: The spec, as applied here. Take one value per calendar day: the first weigh-in after waking and voiding, on the same scale, in minimal clothing (#212, #350, #502, #592). Fit weight = a + b x day (b in kg/day) by ordinary least squares over the trailing window, using only days on or after the date the current target took effect. The observed rate is 7b divided by the fitted weight at the end of the window (today). It is a signed fraction of body weight per week (negative = loss), the same convention as goals.<goal>.weeklyChangeFraction. This matches the engine's weight_trend (latestKg and weeklyChangeFraction) and toleranceFractionPerWeek. The engine implements only this method and does not read this value. Engine gap: weight_trend currently fits every reading and must first keep only the first reading of each day. Do not convert the slope to kcal. The energy density of weight change conflicts across sources: 4,858-6,041 kcal/kg early (#547), rho 8,840 (#552), 9,500/1,020 FM/FFM (#588) and 9,300/1,100 FM/FFM (#818, #557). So the step is a fixed amount, and the slope sets only its direction. End-of-window leverage (my calculation): one reading 1.35% high on the last day (a holiday-sized jump, #590) moves a 15-reading 35-d slope by about 0.10%/wk and a 35-reading slope by about 0.05%/wk. A 1.5 kg creatine-loading gain (#392) in the final week moves a 35-d slope by about 0.36%/wk at 80 kg (0.53%/wk for a 28-d window), which is above the tolerance. The method does not model water shifts. Creatine loading adds 1-2 kg (#392). A carbohydrate diet break added +0.6 kg, seen as FFM (#320). Leaving a ketogenic diet is estimated to add about 1.6-2.5 kg (#583). One trial delayed measurement at least 2 days after a refeed (#328). The luteal phase can add more than 2 kg (#489, second-hand), and a slope over about one menstrual cycle does not cancel it (see windowDays). Glycogen effects fall mostly within about a week (#529). Hall & Chow found their slope-based estimate deviated most just after diet changes, because of body-fluid shifts. Open owner decision: let users flag creatine loading, a refeed or diet break, leaving keto, and menstruation, and drop the affected days (7 days for glycogen events) from the fit. Also start the window 7 days late when the app itself ends a deficit phase (see windowDays). The source is an inpatient trial with complete daily weighing, and Hall & Chow's simulations also assume daily weights. Applying the method to sparse free-living weigh-ins is therefore an extrapolation, and certainty is low. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #819, #818, #557, #589, #590, #592, #262, #434, #489, #212, #350, #502, #599, #593, #552, #547, #588, #529, #392, #320, #583, #328.

intakeLoggingUse.value: displayOnly: logged intake is shown to the user and may prompt an adherence review when the weight trend misses the goal, but it is never used to compute observed energy expenditure, maintenance energy, or the size or direction of any proposed target change; proposals are computed only from the current target and the weigh-in trend
intakeLoggingUse.rationale: NASEM 2023 treats the body-weight trend, not reported intake, as the valid indicator of energy adequacy (#50, high). It also says self-reported intake runs systematically low, more so in women and some higher-BMI groups, and should not be used alone (#51, moderate). Subar 2015 advises never treating self-reported energy as true intake (#622). A rule of 'use logs only when at least N days are logged' was rejected. The error is a bias, not noise, so more days do not remove it. Against doubly labelled water, food records under-reported by 11-41% in 19 studies (#630), and technology-assisted records by 6-37% (#631). People who reported diet resistance under-reported by about 47% (#619, abstract only). In the Burrows review, under-reporting was greater in adults with overweight or obesity, and in women using recall-based methods; the sex difference was inconsistent for food records (#636). NASEM's 31 days of records (#52) buys precision, not freedom from bias. Few users log that much. Under daily prescriptions, only 9% of intervention occasions reached 75% of days (#610), none did so over 12 months or more (#611), and only 15% of interventions averaged 6 or more logged days a week (#613). Logging adherence also falls over time (#606), entries get backfilled (#607), and logging itself changes eating (#629). The safety direction: observed expenditure = logged intake - change in stores. Under-reporting makes computed expenditure too low, so the app would propose lower intake targets, and for a fat-loss user that deepens the deficit. A 20% under-report on 2,500 kcal is 500 kcal/d, five times the adjustment step. Sanghvi puts self-report error at several hundred kcal/d, against a mean bias under 40 kcal/d for the weight-based method (#558). The IOC calls self-reported intake the largest source of error in field estimates of energy availability (#455). Logs still have a use. The common 6-8 month plateau in free-living dieters is more likely due to waning adherence than to metabolic adaptation (#539, #586). So a stalled trend should prompt a review of the log before any further cut. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #50, #51, #52, #630, #631, #622, #558, #636, #619, #610, #611, #613, #606, #607, #629, #455, #728, #625, #539, #586.

defaultPace.rationale:
This is an owner decision; no study compares default adaptation speeds. Standard is the default because it honours the owner's request: the first possible change comes at 4 weeks instead of 5. It is the one window Hall & Chow report directly, and the shortest they judge likely needed (+/-350 kcal/d analytic, 290-300 simulated). In simulation it flags a real miss 2-7 days sooner than slower (medians), and by 16 weeks it has corrected 77-98% as much. Noise does not drive its targets down faster than slower's. An on-goal fat-loss user who accepted every proposal ended the year at a mean change of about -13 to -55 kcal/d, against about -4 to -79 on slower. Its costs are more proposals. An on-goal fat-loss user gets 5.1-5.5 a year at a 1% daily SD, against 1.8-2.7 on slower (0.6-0.7 against 0.1 at 0.625%). A user whose weight swings with the menstrual cycle gets about 10-13 a year with up to 9 reversals of direction, against about 3-6 with up to 4 on slower (illustrative 1 kg swing at 60 kg). The app cannot detect such a swing, so the setup copy recommends slower for it. No 3-week pace is offered. In simulation a 21-day rule either corrected real misses less than slower or, in its best tested form, roughly doubled noise-driven cuts (see standard.windowDays).

The default is deliberately not tied to how fast users feel their metabolism is. In the few small studies that tested such beliefs, they did not match measurement. In Wallhuss 2010, 44 people who felt their metabolism was high and 12 who felt it was low had fasting RMRs of 7,230 vs 7,430 kJ/d (P = 0.6). This compared absolute RMR, and the 'low' group was heavier (BMI 27.8 vs 20.4), so a size-adjusted difference is not excluded. In Lichtman 1992, 10 self-described diet-resistant people had total expenditure and RMR within 5% of prediction from body composition, but under-reported intake by 47% (#619). Clark 1995 is indirect, since it grouped 18 women by how much they felt they ate, not by perceived metabolism. Its 9 self-perceived small eaters had a higher, not lower, FFM-adjusted RMR (3,891 vs 3,375 J/min), though also a higher RQ. Real residual differences do exist. In Anthanont 2016, the top and bottom 15% of 757 weight-stable volunteers had BMRs more than about 169-173 kcal/d above or below the value predicted from fat-free mass, fat mass, age and sex, so about 70% lay within that range. Yet over a mean of about 9.7 years of follow-up, the low-BMR group did not gain weight faster (0.3 vs 0.5 kg/y). Total expenditure also varies by more than +/-20% after adjustment (Pontzer 2021, #128). The weigh-in trend shows the net effect of expenditure and actual intake on the current target, and that is what the suggestions act on. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

windowDays.rationale: Pace paragraph to append. This is the most precise pace. With daily weights, a 0.5 kg weight SD, rho 9,100 kcal/kg and epsilon 22 kcal/kg/d, Hall & Chow's Eq. 3 gives a 95% CI on intake change of about +/-295 kcal/d at 35 d, against +/-352 at 28 d and +/-457 at 21 d (reviewer calculations; the paper itself states +/-350 at 28 d). At a 0.35 kg SD the figures are +/-207, 247 and 320. The equation's epsilon-rho cross term dominates at these lengths, so the variance falls only about 1.4-fold from 28 to 35 d, not the 1.95-fold of the slope term alone. In the engine's own units, the 95% half-width of the weekly slope is 0.23 x the daily SD with daily weights and 0.34 x at the 15-weigh-in minimum (my arithmetic). This window also resists cyclic swings best. With an illustrative 1 kg peak-to-trough, 28-day menstrual swing (#489 reports that the luteal phase can add more than 2 kg; the size is an open gap), the worst-phase slope bias is about 0.08 kg/wk at 35 d, against 0.24 at 28 d and 0.43 at 21 d (my calculation). This is therefore the pace the setup copy recommends when weight swings with the menstrual cycle. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumWeighIns.rationale: Pace paragraph to append. 15 of 35 days is 43% of the window, and the standard pace keeps that share (12 of 28), about 3 weigh-ins a week. So a user who weighs about 3 days a week has a broadly similar chance of qualifying under either pace. With weigh-ins on random days, a single check on this pace qualified 41% of the time at 3 a week, 68% at 3.5 and 86% at 4; on standard it was 46%, 71% and 87-88% (reviewer simulation of the engine's trend rule). Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumWeighInDaysPerWeek.rationale: Unchanged. The rule needs at least 2 weigh-in days in every full 7-day block. Weekend readings go missing most often (#593), and weight follows a weekday cycle (#589), so an uneven spread would bias the slope. The rule also keeps the 15 weigh-ins from bunching. At the most clustered spread the rule allows, the slope half-width is 0.54 x the daily SD, against 0.34 x when evenly spread (my arithmetic). Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

toleranceFractionPerWeek.rationale: Unchanged. This is the reference band that the standard pace widens from. At the 15-weigh-in minimum, the one-sided chance that an on-goal fat-loss user gets an 'eat less' proposal from noise alone at one check is about 0.2%, 1.0% and 7.3% at daily SDs of 0.5%, 0.625% (0.5 kg at 80 kg) and 1% of body weight (my arithmetic). Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

adjustmentStepKcal.rationale: Pace paragraph to append. 100 kcal per 35 days sets the reference maximum rate of change, about 2.9 kcal/d per day, and the standard pace keeps it (80 kcal per 28 d). So both paces can move targets toward the goal by about the same total over a phase: at most 300 kcal/d on slower (days 35, 70 and 105) and 320 on standard (days 28, 56, 84 and 112) in 16 weeks. They differ in how early the steps come and how small they are. The bound covers goal-direction proposals, which wait out minimumDaysBetweenAdjustments. A 'losing faster than safe' proposal can come sooner, but it only ever raises intake. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumDaysBetweenAdjustments.rationale: Unchanged, with the correction above. Setting it equal to windowDays means every goal-direction proposal is judged on a full window recorded entirely under the current target, so an accepted change cannot be counted twice. The 35-day spacing also moves each check a week later in a roughly 28-day menstrual cycle (#489), so successive checks do not land on the same phase. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

windowDays.rationale:
No source sets a trend window for an adaptive app, so this is an owner decision. Twenty-eight days is the one window Hall & Chow report directly. With 28 daily weights, a 0.5 kg SD, rho 9,100 kcal/kg and epsilon 22 kcal/kg/d, the intake-change estimate has an SD of 180 kcal/d and a 95% CI of +/-350. Their three simulated free-living subjects gave 95% CIs of 290-300 kcal/d. The authors judge that daily weights over at least 28 d are likely needed to assess diet adherence, and their abstract says more than 28 d was needed for a CI under 300. So 28 d is the likely minimum by the paper's own standard, not a comfortable margin. Precision given up against slower (reviewer Eq. 3 values, daily weights): +/-352 vs +/-295 kcal/d at a 0.5 kg SD and +/-247 vs +/-207 at 0.35 kg, about 19% wider. In the engine's slope units, the 95% half-width is 0.32 x vs 0.23 x the daily SD with daily weights, and 0.47 x vs 0.34 x at each pace's minimum count (my arithmetic). Weekly cycle: a 0.35% Monday-to-Friday swing (#589) leaves a worst-phase slope residual of 0.021%/wk over 4 whole weeks. Cadence precedents: MATADOR recalculated the prescription every 4 weeks (#304), and ACSM describes progress toward short-term goals over about 3-6 weeks (#346). Early transients: glycogen and water act mainly in the first week (#529), and early loss has a low energy density until weeks 4-6 (#547). Hall & Chow saw their largest errors just after diet changes. At 28 d the first week is a quarter of the window, against a fifth at 35 d.

What the shorter window buys (simulation, every proposal accepted): a fat-loss user whose weight is flat gets a first cut at day 28 instead of 35. From about day 35, slower's larger steps catch up. By day 112 this pace has cut that user by 214-244 kcal/d, against 240-288 on slower. The correction comes a week sooner but is not larger.

Menstrual caveat: with an illustrative 1 kg peak-to-trough swing (#489; the size is an open gap), the worst-phase slope bias is 0.24 kg/wk. At 60 kg that is 0.40%/wk, which exceeds this pace's 0.3%/wk tolerance. And 28-day spacing can put successive checks on the same phase of a roughly 28-day cycle, so the bias can repeat. For a 60-kg on-goal fat-loss user with that swing, with proposals declined, this pace gave 4.4-6.2 'eat less' and 3.7-8.5 'losing faster than safe, eat more' proposals a year, about 10-13 in all. Slower gave 2.9-4.2 and 0.6-1.3, about 3.7-5.1 in all. With every proposal accepted, this pace gave 9.8-12.8 proposals a year with 4-9 reversals of direction, against 2.9-6.4 and 1-4 on slower. The year's net change stayed within about +/-160 kcal/d (5th-95th percentile). Hence the setup copy points such users to slower.

No shorter pace is offered. At 21 d, Eq. 3 gives +/-457 kcal/d at a 0.5 kg SD, and 21 d is below the 28 d the paper judges likely needed. In 46 free-living adults not trying to change weight, the change between two weighings 2 weeks apart had an SD of 1.1-1.3 kg. About 84% of it was fat-free mass, at about 2,380 kcal/kg. The authors conclude that weight change alone cannot be expected to separate energy balance from a sustained imbalance under 500 kcal/d in an individual (Bhutani 2017). That was a two-point change, not a daily-weight trend, so it is indirect support. In simulation with every proposal accepted, the drafted 21-day pace (0.4%/wk band, 60 kcal step) corrected real misses less than slower from day 42 on. By day 112 it had cut a flat-weight fat-loss user by 150-214 kcal/d (slower 240-288), and it made 2.3-13 proposals a year to an on-goal fat-loss user (slower 0.1-2.7). The best 21-day variant tested (0.3%/wk band, 80 kcal step, loss ceiling judged on slower's trend, which needs an engine change) did correct more than slower. But noise then cut an on-goal fat-loss user's target by about 100-170 kcal/d a year, against about 5-80 on slower, with 1.9-7.7 proposals a year. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumWeighIns.rationale: No source gives a minimum count, so this is an owner decision. It keeps the slower pace's 43% share of days (15/35 = 12/28), about 3 weigh-ins a week. Adherence: trials instructing daily weighing averaged 44%, 50% and 95% of days, about 3.1, 3.5 and 6.7 a week (#599). Under daily prescriptions, 65% of weight-tracking interventions averaged at least half of days logged (#612). NoHoW participants managed about 4 a week at first, falling to about 2.5 over 2 years (#593). About half of daily-tracking interventions averaged at least 4 logged days a week, though that counts all tracked behaviours, not weighing alone (#613). With weigh-ins on random days, a single check qualified 46% of the time at 3 a week (41% on slower), 71% at 3.5 and 87-88% at 4 (reviewer simulation). Precision: 12 evenly spread weigh-ins give a slope half-width of 0.47 x the daily SD per week, against 0.32 x with daily weights. More weigh-ins still help, as Hall & Chow and Sanghvi (#556) note, but window length matters more than count. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumWeighInDaysPerWeek.rationale: Same reasoning as slower: weekend readings go missing most often (#593), and a weekday weight cycle (#589) means an uneven spread biases the slope. At the most clustered spread the rule allows, the 28-day slope half-width is 0.79 x the daily SD, against 0.47 x when evenly spread (my arithmetic). Without the rule the spread could be worse still. Raising it to 3 would drop many windows for people who average 3 weigh-ins a week. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

toleranceFractionPerWeek.rationale:
No source defines a tolerance band, so this is an owner decision. It is widened from 0.0025 because the 28-day slope is noisier: at the minimum count its SD is 0.2385 x the daily SD per week, against 0.172 x for slower (1.38x). For one check by an on-goal fat-loss user, the one-sided chance of a noise-only 'eat less' proposal is 0.6%, 2.2% and 10.4% at daily SDs of 0.5%, 0.625% and 1%, against 0.2%, 1.0% and 7.3% for slower. Fully matching slower would need about 0.0035. In simulation (proposals declined), 0.0035 flagged partial misses later than slower in most cases. Fat loss at half the goal rate was flagged later in 3 of the 4 noise cases (median 39, 42 and 37 days against 38, 36 and 36), and sooner only at a 1% SD on half the days (36 against 39). At a 0.625% SD a stalled gainer was flagged at 39-41 days against 36-38 (at a 1% SD it was sooner, 33-35 against 35.5-39). That defeats the purpose of the pace. At 0.003 the first flag came sooner than on slower in all four noise cases: a fat-loss stall at a median day 28 against 35, half the goal rate at 33-34 against 36-39, and a muscle-gain stall at 30-34 against 35.5-39.

The total correction is similar, not larger. With every proposal accepted and weight responding at 7,700 kcal/kg, by day 112 this pace had cut a flat-weight fat-loss user by 214-244 kcal/d (slower 240-288). It cut a user losing at half the goal rate by 125-169 (slower 147-176) and raised a stalled gainer by 138-166 (slower 152-184). That is 77-98% of slower's correction.

Noise: an on-goal fat-loss user who accepted every proposal ended the year at a mean change of about -13, -28 and -55 kcal/d in the three noise cases (5th percentile -80 to -160), against about -4, -56 and -70 to -79 on slower (5th percentile 0 to -200). So the wider band and the 80 kcal step keep noise from deepening the deficit faster than on slower. (Counting 'eat less' proposals in declined runs and multiplying by the step gives a gross proxy that is 1.2x slower's at a 1% SD on half the days, 1.6x with daily weighing and 2-4x at a 0.625% SD; it ignores the weight response and opposing proposals.) The cost is frequency: 0.6-5.5 proposals a year with 0.2-3.0 reversals of direction, against 0.1-2.7 and 0-1.2 on slower. About half the extra come from the loss ceiling (see minimumWeighIns).

The price of the wider band is sensitivity. The smallest real fat-loss shortfall that triggers is 0.24 kg/wk at 80 kg, about 207-264 kcal/d at 6,041-7,700 kcal/kg (#547). That is below the intake uncertainty of a 28-day window (+/-350 kcal/d in Hall & Chow), so a single check cannot reliably separate such a shortfall from noise; repeated checks do. For muscle gain the trigger sits just below zero slope (-0.05%/wk), so a flat trend is flagged only when noise pushes the fitted slope below that; in simulation stalled gainers were still flagged sooner than on slower. The 80 kcal step is below the smallest triggering fat-loss shortfall even at 50 kg (129-165 kcal/d). So one step does not overshoot a real deviation that triggers, for users of about 50 kg or more. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

adjustmentStepKcal.rationale: No source prescribes a trend-adjustment step. NASEM says to adjust intake incrementally but gives no size (#50). The one number is a 100-200 kcal/d taper for lean bodybuilders (#227, narrative review). I chose 80 so that the maximum rate of change matches the reviewed slower pace: 100 kcal per 35 d and 80 per 28 d are both about 2.9 kcal/d per day. A 16-week phase then allows at most 4 goal-direction changes (days 28, 56, 84 and 112), 320 kcal/d in total, against 300 on slower. On either pace, loss-ceiling 'eat more' proposals skip the wait and only raise intake. So this pace moves sooner, not further: in simulation with every proposal accepted, by day 112 it had made 77-98% of slower's correction of real misses (see toleranceFractionPerWeek). The smaller step cuts the cost of each noise-driven proposal by 20%, which matters because this pace re-checks sooner and its window is noisier. The step is well below the individual precision of weight-based estimates (RMS 215 kcal/d, #553; Hall & Chow +/-350 kcal/d at 28 d), which limits the cost of a false trigger. It is also below the smallest fat-loss shortfall that triggers (129-165 kcal/d at 50 kg, #547), so one step does not overshoot a real deviation that triggers. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

minimumDaysBetweenAdjustments.rationale: Same logic as slower: with spacing below the window, the deviation behind the last accepted change would still sit in the next window and could trigger a second change in the same direction. Four-weekly recalculation has trial precedent in MATADOR (#304), and ACSM describes a 3-6 week horizon for short-term goals (#346). Caveat: in a user with a roughly 28-day cycle, 28-day spacing can put successive checks on the same menstrual phase (#489), so a cycle-driven bias can repeat. That is why slower remains the recommended pace for users whose weight swings with their cycle. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

value.question: How soon should the app suggest calorie changes from your weigh-ins?
value.slower: Can suggest a change after 5 weeks of regular weigh-ins, then at most every 5 weeks. The most reliable, and the better choice if your weight swings with your menstrual cycle.
value.standard: Can suggest a change after 4 weeks of regular weigh-ins, then at most every 4 weeks. A week sooner than the slower pace, in slightly smaller steps, but a little less certain.
value.perceivedMetabolismNote: In the few small studies that have tested it, people's sense of having a fast or slow metabolism did not match their measured metabolic rate, so it is not a reliable guide. Real differences between people do exist. On either pace, suggestions follow how your weight actually changes on your current targets, so choose a pace for how soon you want changes. On either pace, the app may suggest eating more sooner if you are losing weight faster than is safe.

paceCopy.rationale: Setup-screen wording for the pace choice, summarising the pace research: self-perceived metabolism did not match measured metabolic rate (Wallhuss 2010, Lichtman 1992, Clark 1995); individual differences exist (Pontzer 2021, Anthanont 2016) and are revealed by the weight trend. Pace research: docs/research/diet-evidence.json (paceResearch).

intakeNote.value: Logged food is shown against your targets, but it never changes them: food logs usually under-count what was eaten, so targets adapt to your weight trend instead.
intakeNote.rationale: NASEM 2023 treats the body-weight trend, not reported intake, as the valid indicator of energy adequacy (#50, high). It also says self-reported intake runs systematically low, more so in women and some higher-BMI groups, and should not be used alone (#51, moderate). Subar 2015 advises never treating self-reported energy as true intake (#622). A rule of 'use logs only when at least N days are logged' was rejected. The error is a bias, not noise, so more days do not remove it. Against doubly labelled water, food records under-reported by 11-41% in 19 studies (#630), and technology-assisted records by 6-37% (#631). People who reported diet resistance under-reported by about 47% (#619, abstract only). In the Burrows review, under-reporting was greater in adults with overweight or obesity, and in women using recall-based methods; the sex difference was inconsistent for food records (#636). NASEM's 31 days of records (#52) buys precision, not freedom from bias. Few users log that much. Under daily prescriptions, only 9% of intervention occasions reached 75% of days (#610), none did so over 12 months or more (#611), and only 15% of interventions averaged 6 or more logged days a week (#613). Logging adherence also falls over time (#606), entries get backfilled (#607), and logging itself changes eating (#629). The safety direction: observed expenditure = logged intake - change in stores. Under-reporting makes computed expenditure too low, so the app would propose lower intake targets, and for a fat-loss user that deepens the deficit. A 20% under-report on 2,500 kcal is 500 kcal/d, five times the adjustment step. Sanghvi puts self-report error at several hundred kcal/d, against a mean bias under 40 kcal/d for the weight-based method (#558). The IOC calls self-reported intake the largest source of error in field estimates of energy availability (#455). Logs still have a use. The common 6-8 month plateau in free-living dieters is more likely due to waning adherence than to metabolic adaptation (#539, #586). So a stalled trend should prompt a review of the log before any further cut. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #50, #51, #52, #630, #631, #622, #558, #636, #619, #610, #611, #613, #606, #607, #629, #455, #728, #625, #539, #586.

minimumAgeYears.rationale: No source sets a minimum age for a consumer diet-target app, so this is an owner decision. The profile stores only the birth year. The engine computes age as the current calendar year minus the birth year (diet.age_years), and the same age goes into the EER equation. With a threshold of 19, the youngest user admitted was born on 31 December nineteen years before the current year, and is 18 years and 1 day old on 1 January. So 19 is the smallest whole number that admits no one under 18. A threshold of 18 would admit 17-year-olds for part of every year. Every adult reference value the engine uses is defined for ages 19 and over: the NASEM 2023 EER equations for men and women (#43, #44), their SEPV (#47) and PAL bands (#45), and the IOM protein RDA (#62), carbohydrate RDA (#68), iron (#701) and calcium (#712) values. The DRI places people who are truly 18 in the 14-18 y life stage, where the values differ. IOM 2011 Table S-1, the table behind #712, sets the calcium RDA at 1,300 mg/d for 14-18 y and 1,000 mg/d for 19-30 y (checked in the saved Summary text). No adolescent energy equation is among the verified findings. Pontzer (#126) puts the adult plateau of size-adjusted TEE at about 20.5 y (95% CI 19.8-21.2), and 20-25-year-olds averaged 102.7% of the adult-expected value. So adult equations may slightly underestimate need in the late teens and early twenties, which errs toward too large a deficit. That applies to 19- and 20-year-olds as well. It argues for caution near the boundary, but it does not favour 19 over 18, and the energy floors and the deficit cap limit that error. AAP 2016 (#752, #753; abstract only, no age cut-off) says guidance for adolescents should focus on habits rather than weight, because some teens who try to lose weight develop eating disorders. The Triad statement judges adolescent energy stores by % of expected weight rather than by adult BMI cut-offs (#472), and IOC 2023 allows body-composition assessment under 18 only for medical reasons (#450). Together these support excluding everyone under 18, and 19 is the value that does this when only the birth year is known. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #43, #44, #45, #47, #62, #68, #701, #712, #126, #752, #753, #472, #450.

exclusions.rationale: The list combines exclusions backed by guidelines with conservative owner decisions where the research has gaps. The support for each item follows. underMinimumAge: see safety.minimumAgeYears (#43, #44, #126, #752, #753, #472, #450). pregnancy: IOM 2009 sets a positive gain range and a weekly gain rate for every pre-pregnancy BMI (#748, #749, #750) and gives no safe rate of loss (#751). eatingDisorderRisk (a positive screen): SCOFF accuracy (#738, #739, #740, #741); NICE says to tailor care or refer for eating disorders (#770); IOC 2010 says to refer people at risk (#366). eatingDisorderHistory (a self-reported diagnosis or treatment): IOC 2023 CAT2 counts a diagnosed eating disorder as a primary indicator (#447); the Triad statement requires physician, dietitian and mental-health care for a clinical eating disorder (#481); NICE says to tailor or refer (#770); aggressive dieting raises the risk of binge eating and food preoccupation (#229). SCOFF sensitivity is only 0.71-0.77 in community samples, samples with more men, and samples that include binge eating disorder (#739), so a known diagnosis must gate on its own. Including past eating disorders is the conservative owner choice. chronicKidneyDisease: the KDIGO 2024 definition, GFR <60 and/or ACR >=30 mg/g for >=3 months, or a transplant history (#744); protein 0.8 g/kg in G3-G5, and avoid >1.3 g/kg (#743, #742); renal dietitian input (#745); PROT-AGE CKD limits (#184). Devries (#187) shows the protein-safety evidence covers only adults without CKD. type1Diabetes: carbohydrate intake and insulin dosing are linked and individual, and glucose and ketone thresholds are clinical decisions (#754, #755, #756); NICE lists T1D as needing tailored care (#770). lowBmi: BMI <=17.5 is a proposed low-energy-availability warning sign (#457) and the Triad high-risk score (#474). The Triad text flag is <17.5 (#472), so <=17.5 is the inclusive, conservative reading. <=75% of median BMI is an IOC urgent-care flag (#448). BMI 17.5 to <18.5 scores moderate risk (#474) and sits below the FAO healthy range (#39); that band belongs to a fat-loss BMI floor, not to this list, which withholds all targets. rapidRecentWeightLoss: >=10% in a month is Triad high risk (#474) and an IOC 2018 LEA indicator (#456). missedPeriods: in IOC 2023 CAT2, secondary amenorrhoea of 3-11 missed cycles is a primary indicator and 12 or more is a severe primary indicator (#447); fewer than 6 menses a year is Triad high risk (#476); finding one Triad component should prompt evaluation for the others (#481); ACSM 2016 links sustained EA below 30 kcal/kg FFM/d to impaired body functions and reports menses returning once EA was raised to about 40 (#192). clinicianManagedDiet: NICE requires tailoring or referral for IBD, MASLD, coeliac disease and similar conditions (#770), and KDIGO asks for dietitian input in CKD (#745). The remaining items are owner decisions for gaps. lactation: the verified findings cover pregnancy only (#748-#751). hypoglycaemiaRiskMedication: extrapolated from the T1D consensus (#754, #756); from AHA 2013, which says larger weight losses reduce medication needs, so doses need clinical review (#782); and from NICE, which places low-energy diets for type 2 diabetes inside long-term-condition services (#766). glp1Therapy: larger deficits cost lean mass (#240, #232), rapid loss raises gallstone risk (#791, #792), and NICE requires supervision for low-energy intakes (#765, #766, #767). bariatricSurgery: no finding covers it directly; energy restriction raises the risk of micronutrient deficiency (#359). Withholding targets is the safe direction for every gap item. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #43, #44, #126, #752, #753, #472, #450, #748, #749, #750, #751, #738, #739, #740, #741, #770, #366, #447, #481, #229, #742, #743, #744, #745, #184, #187, #754, #755, #756, #782, #766, #765, #767, #240, #232, #791, #792, #359, #457, #474, #448, #39, #456, #476, #192.

scoff.locator: Kutz 2020 J Gen Intern Med: Results 'Diagnostic accuracy' (pooled sensitivity 0.86, specificity 0.83; threshold effect r=-0.21, p=0.32); Table 3 subgroup analyses (community, <60% female, binge eating disorder, North America); Discussion and Conclusions (large-scale screening in primary care and community settings). Item content and scoring rule (one point per yes, score >=2): Morgan 1999 BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj.319.7223.1467, PMID 10582927), box of questions and footnote.
scoff.note: Scoring: 1 point per 'yes', 0-5 in total. diet.safety_block compares scoffYesCount >= referralScore, so a score of 2 or more triggers eatingDisorderRisk and a referral message. The cut-off of 2 is kept for four reasons: Morgan 1999 defines it (#740); USPSTF 2022 pooled adult accuracy at >=2 (#741, abstract only: sensitivity 84%, specificity 80%, 10 studies); Kutz found no threshold effect (#738); and no verified finding supports a cut-off of 1. I lowered certainty from moderate to low, as one review asked. The other two reviews noted that moderate is allowed for a meta-analysis. That is true, but the grade should reflect how well the value fits this use. The reasons for low: Morgan's cut-off comes from a case-control derivation in 116 women with anorexia or bulimia and 96 female college controls (checked in the saved full text). In community samples, which is this app's setting, Kutz found sensitivity 0.71; it was 0.75 in samples with more men, 0.77 with binge eating disorder included and 0.69 in North America (#739). Kutz pooled 25 studies with I2 about 98%, only two of them rated low on every risk-of-bias and applicability domain (#738), and concluded there is insufficient evidence to recommend the SCOFF for large-scale screening in primary care and diverse community settings (Discussion, saved full text). The questions are paraphrased, as the brief asked, but the validated accuracy applies only to the original wording. So a negative score is not clearance. The screen is one layer of the safety gate, alongside the self-reported eatingDisorderHistory exclusion. The owner must accept that the paraphrase is unvalidated or have it checked. Item 3 unit fix, accepted from all reviews: the draft's '6 kg (about 14 lb)' mixed two thresholds, because 6 kg is 13.2 lb and 14 lb is one stone (6.35 kg). It now reads 6 kg (13 lb). Since 13 lb is 5.9 kg, both units sit just below one stone, so both are slightly more sensitive than the original. Users already losing weight on purpose may answer yes to item 3 (#740). The conservative choice is to count that answer anyway and to run the screen at onboarding, before any weight loss driven by the app. A user losing about 0.5 kg a week passes 6 kg within 3 months, so a later re-screen would flag some users who are on plan; that errs toward withholding. Whether to re-screen, and how often, is an owner decision. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #738, #739, #740, #741.

energyAvailabilityFloorKcalPerKgFFM.locator: Mountjoy 2023 IOC REDs consensus, Br J Sports Med 57(17): Clinical applications > Assessment of EA (pp.1078, 1080; zones: 30-45 reduced EA for mass/fat loss, <=30 LEA with health implications); Key scientific advances > REDs in male athletes (p.1077); Clinical applications > Body composition assessment and management (pp.1080, 1082-1083)
energyAvailabilityFloorKcalPerKgFFM.note: EA = (daily energy intake - exercise energy expenditure) / fat-free mass, in kcal/kg FFM/day. Engine behaviour, corrected from the draft as two reviews asked: diet.energy_floor applies this floor whenever the user has entered a body-fat percentage, with FFM = latest weight x (1 - bodyFatPercent/100). Exercise energy is not measured, so it counts as zero and the floor is 30 x FFM kcal/d. This is a necessary lower bound, not the full EA floor. Intake must be at least 30 x FFM plus the day's exercise energy, so for active users EA at the engine floor is below 30. Example: FFM 45 kg gives an engine floor of 1,350 kcal/d, but with 300 kcal/d of exercise the full EA floor is 30 x 45 + 300 = 1,650 kcal/d. The draft said to skip the check when exercise energy is missing; keep the engine's behaviour instead, because a floor that ignores exercise still protects more than no floor. The check is skipped, and recorded as unassessed, only when body fat is missing; the absolute floor and the deficit cap then apply alone. Where exercise energy could come from (logged sessions, MET estimates or HealthKit) is an open gap. Adding it would raise this floor, and using HealthKit for it needs an owner ruling under AGENTS.md rule 4. Boundary: IOC 2023, the main source, puts <=30 in the LEA zone with health implications and 30-45 in the reduced zone used for fat loss (#442). ACSM 2016 and IOC 2018 use <30 instead (#344, #192, #454), and Loucks 2003 found LH pulsatility intact after 5 days at 30 kcal/kg LBM/day and disrupted below that (#464). Under the conservative rule the bound is exclusive: EA must stay above 30. One review argued for an inclusive bound because EA measurement error is far larger than 1 kcal/kg. That is true, but it does not make the less conservative reading preferable. The value stays 30. The engine currently clamps to exactly 30 x FFM and rounds to the nearest 10 kcal, so a binding floor can land up to 5 kcal (under 0.2 kcal/kg FFM) below it. Rounding up to the next 10 kcal whenever a floor binds would keep the target above the bound. That gap is far smaller than the uncounted exercise energy. Sex: in men, symptoms appear at lower EA, about 9-25 (#443) or below 25 (#246); about 20-25 may be pathological in bodybuilders (#460); and male thresholds are unknown (#459). I apply 30 to both sexes as the more conservative value. Other support: the Triad statement (#468) and Schofield (#104). IOC 2023 says the zones come from small, short studies in sedentary women and are a guide, not a diagnostic endpoint (#442). Lieberman 2018, Med Sci Sports Exerc, doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000001451, PMID 29023359: I checked the PubMed abstract on 2026-09-24. It is not yet a finding, so the owner should add it before citing it. In a secondary analysis of an RCT in 35 sedentary, ovulatory women aged 18-24, the odds of menstrual disturbance fell 9% for each unit increase in EA (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84-0.98), and no threshold emerged. So 30 is not a safe line. The app uses it only as a clamp that raises a target, and never tells a user they have low energy availability or REDs. Never estimate FFM or body fat from BMI, age or sex equations. IOC 2023 judges easy-to-use 'doubly indirect' methods, which derive body fat from regression equations, to be invalid (#450), and the open questions list no validated method for an app. Consumer bioimpedance scales use such equations, so treat a body-fat % the user enters as low-validity. If body fat is overestimated, FFM and the floor come out too low, and the check may not bind. That is why the check only ever raises targets and never relaxes the other floors. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #442, #443, #344, #192, #454, #464, #468, #104, #246, #460, #459, #450.

maximumDeficitFractionOfTEE.rationale: No source gives a maximum deficit as a fraction of TEE, so this is an owner decision. The evidence behind it follows. AHA 2013 accepts deficits of 500-750 kcal/d for adults with overweight or obesity, and its evidence statement also lists a 30% deficit (#780). Two trials in resistance-trained adults, described as lean in #326 and #724, prescribed 25% below maintenance. In Conlin 2021 (about 18-20% achieved over 10 weeks), fat-free mass was maintained and about 98% of the loss was fat (#722, #724). In Campbell 2020 (21% achieved in the continuous arm and 26% in the refeed arm, over 7 weeks; #326), the continuous -25% arm lost 1.3 kg FFM and 1.9 kg dry FFM within-group (#325), so 25% is not free of lean-mass cost. In Garthe 2011, elite athletes who cut intake by about 19% gained lean mass, and those who cut about 30% did not (#217, #218). Murphy 2022 found that a deficit of about 500 kcal/d prevented lean-mass gains (#240), and ACSM 2016 advises 250-500 kcal/d (#346, #194). At TEEs of 2,000-3,000 kcal, 25% equals 500-750 kcal, which spans the AHA range; at a TEE of 2,000 it equals the Murphy ceiling. NASEM's starting rule, EER - 1.96 x SEPV (#48, #47), is a fixed 670 kcal/d for men and 472 for women. That is about 22% for the report's example man (EER 3,041) and about 21% for its example woman (EER 2,275). It exceeds 25% only when EER is below about 2,680 kcal/d for men or 1,890 for women. The 33% deficit (MATADOR, obese men on provided food, #304) and the ~40% deficit (Longland, a 4-week diet provided by the researchers, #167) come from supervised trials that do not apply to an unsupervised app. The value 0.25 is below the 30% that AHA lists and that Garthe's fast arm used. It equals the largest deficit prescribed in the trials of resistance-trained adults, and one of those arms lost some FFM. So 0.25 is a ceiling at the edge of the tested range, not a default that is safe for lean mass. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #780, #722, #724, #326, #325, #217, #218, #240, #232, #346, #194, #304, #167, #48, #47, #50, #768.

minimumEnergyKcal.rationale: Men 1,500 kcal/d and women 1,200 kcal/d are the lower ends of the AHA/ACC/TOS 2013 guideline's diet ranges (Jensen 2013, Table 4 recommendation 3a; finding #779). NICE NG246 (finding #766) classes 800-1,200 kcal/d, including 1,200 itself, as a low-energy diet for specialist services only. To stay outside that band the women's floor is set just above it: 1,210 kcal, the lowest value the engine can show at its 10-kcal rounding. NICE NG246 is an official guideline without a DOI or PMID, so it is recorded here as an owner decision rather than as a cited source. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #779, #766.

proteinMultiplier.note: Value 1.0 (no adjustment). AND 2016 (full text read) gives no adult protein multiplier for vegetarians, including athletes: varied plant proteins eaten over the day meet needs when energy intake is adequate (finding 646). IOM 2005 is reported to set no separate requirement for vegetarians who eat complementary plant proteins (finding 72), and Neufingerl 2022 confirms that WHO and IOM specify no increase (finding 682). The IOM pages could not be read (the NAP reader serves page images only), so IOM is corroboration, not the cited locator. A lacto-ovo diet also includes dairy and egg protein, which have the highest leucine density (ISSN 2017, finding 153). Across RCTs the protein source made no significant difference to absolute lean mass or strength, with or without resistance training (Lim 2021 meta-analysis, findings 835 and 839; Messina 2018 soy-vs-animal meta-analysis, findings 641-642, small trials, first author with soy-industry ties). The Lim null for absolute lean mass is fragile: dropping any one of three trials made it significant for animal protein (WMD 0.25-0.29 kg; finding 835). The conflict points upward. Neufingerl 2022 cites proposals of about 20% more protein; with vegetarian diet protein quality put at ~90%, that works out to roughly 1.1x (finding 682; the 1.1 is our arithmetic, not the review's). Lim 2021 also found a small, fragile animal-protein advantage in percent lean mass (+0.50%, no longer significant when any one of four trials was dropped; finding 836). The Nunes 2022 g/kg thresholds come mostly from animal-protein trials (65 of 74; finding 161). The uplift proposals are second-hand and framed at RDA level, and observed vegetarian intakes (13.4% of energy) already exceed a 20% uplift on the 10% AMDR floor (finding 681). Safety: protein has no UL (IOM, finding 63), though IOM notes that this does not show chronic high intakes are tolerated. An uplift would raise the target for every vegetarian user; KDIGO 2024 advises adults with CKD at risk of progression to avoid more than 1.3 g/kg/day (finding 742). Diagnosed CKD is outside the app's scope and handled by exclusion, so this is a direction, not a binding limit: as far as the conservative-for-safety rule applies, it points to 1.0, the same answer as the evidence hierarchy. Protein quality is handled through food suggestions, not a higher target. Source equivalence was shown only at total intakes of about 1.0 g/kg/day or more (finding 840); if any goal ever uses a base target below 1.0 g/kg/day, the owner should revisit this value. Graded low: the AND finding is graded low, the position stand reports no adult trial of a multiplier, and the open-questions file lists the vegetarian/vegan protein adjustment as unresolved. Review changes: primary source moved from IOM 2005 (unverified pages) to AND 2016; 'not a safety parameter' replaced by the safety reasoning above; Lim fragility added. Corroborated by Neufingerl & Eilander 2022 (doi:10.3390/nu14010029) section 4.3, paragraph 2 (WHO and IOM specify no increase). IOM 2005 (doi:10.17226/10490) Ch. 10 agrees, but its cited pp. 661-662 were not verified.
proteinMultiplier.note: Value 1.0 (no adjustment), held with less confidence than the vegetarian value. For 1.0: AND 2016 (full text read) gives no adult multiplier; its 15-35% uplifts are for vegan children only (finding 646). IOM 2005 is reported to set no separate requirement when plant proteins are complementary (finding 72), and Neufingerl 2022 confirms that WHO and IOM specify no increase (finding 682). The IOM pages could not be read, so IOM is corroboration only. The Lim 2021 meta-analysis found no significant difference in absolute lean mass (WMD 0.22 kg, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.46) or strength (findings 835, 839), but that null is fragile: dropping any one of three trials made it significant (WMD 0.25-0.29 kg). Messina 2018 found soy not significantly different from animal protein for lean mass and 1RM (findings 641-643; small trials, within-arm comparisons, first author with soy-industry ties). Hevia-Larrain 2021 matched vegans and omnivores at ~1.6 g/kg/day and found the same leg lean-mass gain (+1.2 kg each); it is a single non-randomised trial in untrained men, read from the abstract and trial registry (findings 638-640). The conflict points upward. Neufingerl 2022 cites proposals of about 20% more protein because vegan diet protein quality is put at ~80% (e.g. 12% of energy instead of 10%), which implies about 1.2-1.25x (finding 682; the 1.25 is our arithmetic). Pinckaers 2021, a narrative review, calls the question unresolved and speculates, without testing, that quality matters more in a calorie deficit (finding 664). Lim 2021 found +0.50% percent lean mass for animal protein, which lost significance when any one of four trials was dropped (finding 836). Only 9 of 74 RCTs in Nunes 2022 used plant protein (finding 161). Whole legumes deliver about 50-75% absorbable protein, against 85-95% for egg and chicken (finding 663). Most plant-protein arms in the Lim 2021 trials used soy, and Hevia-Larrain used soy isolate (findings 835, 640), so evidence for whole-food vegan diets is thinner. Safety: protein has no UL (finding 63), though IOM notes that this does not show chronic high intakes are tolerated. An uplift would raise the target for every vegan user; KDIGO 2024 advises adults with CKD at risk of progression to avoid more than 1.3 g/kg/day (finding 742). Diagnosed CKD is outside the app's scope and handled by exclusion, so this is a direction, not a binding limit: as far as the conservative-for-safety rule applies, it points to 1.0, the same answer as the evidence hierarchy (position stand, DRI corroboration and meta-analyses). Food suggestions should make up for lower protein quality. Combine legume-type and grain-type proteins: in modelling, a 1:1 blend of corn, hemp or brown rice with soy or pea needs 1.1-1.9x the protein of a reference source, against 2-4x for corn, hemp, brown rice, soy or pea alone and 3-8x for oat, lupin, quinoa or wheat alone (finding 661; modelled, not trial-tested). Favour soy and pea, and use larger per-meal plant servings to reach ~2.7 g leucine (finding 659). If the owner wants an uplift, the only cited figure is ~1.2x: second-hand, framed at RDA level, low certainty. Source equivalence was shown only at total intakes of about 1.0 g/kg/day or more (finding 840); if any goal ever uses a base target below 1.0 g/kg/day, the owner should revisit this value. Graded low: the position stand reports no adult trial of a multiplier, and the open-questions file lists the vegan protein adjustment as unresolved. Review changes: primary source moved to AND 2016; Messina wording corrected from 'equal' to 'not significantly different'; the unsupported 'most trials used soy isolate' claim narrowed; 2-4x vs 3-8x single-source factors stated in full; Lim fragility and safety reasoning added. flexibleVsRigid.value: Letting dieters pick their own foods within daily energy and macronutrient targets produced the same weight and fat loss as a dietitian-set fixed meal plan. This was a 10-week RCT in resistance-trained adults (Conlin 2021): fat mass -2.3 kg flexible vs -3.2 kg rigid, with no significant between-group difference on any measure. The trial was small (23 completers, about 40% attrition) and showed no adherence advantage. In observational data, flexible restraint predicted better maintenance of weight loss. Rigid restraint predicted smaller losses and went with more attentional bias toward food and body-shape cues (Westenhoefer 2013; abstract only). In one comparison of four diets, adherence predicted weight loss (r = 0.60) and diet type did not (r = 0.07) (Dansinger 2005). Guidelines name no single superior macronutrient pattern (NICE NG246; AHA/ACC/TOS 2013). Letting people choose between two diet patterns did not improve adherence or weight loss at 48 weeks (Yancy 2015). Use: offer food suggestions within targets rather than fixed meal plans, because outcomes were equivalent, fixed plans showed no advantage, and rigid rules carry a correlational risk. Do not claim that flexible choice improves adherence, results or muscle gain.

flexibleVsRigid.note: No synthesis compares flexible food choice with rigid meal plans directly. The one RCT is small and lost about 40% of participants, and the Westenhoefer data are observational and were read from the abstract only. The evidence supports suggestions as non-inferior to fixed plans, not superior. Do not cite Conlin's post-diet fat-free-mass result (+1.7 kg flexible vs -0.7 kg rigid): the authors decline to attribute it to diet assignment. Two narrative reviews (Iraki 2019; Helms 2014) link cutting out food groups and eating the same few foods to micronutrient shortfalls, which also favours varied suggestions. The populations studied were resistance-trained adults aged 18-39 and women maintaining weight loss; the finding is untested in other groups. No reviewer objection was raised; the draft is kept unchanged. Findings: docs/research/diet-evidence.json #721, #722, #730, #736, #737, #717, #718, #719, #731, #732, #769, #790, #269, #230.
